Introduction India carries a quarter of the global TB burden.1 Undernutrition, which is associated with 1 increased disease severity and unfavorable outcomes, is the leading driver for TB in India.2 Poor 2 weight gain is associated with increased mortality whereas gaining at least 5% of baseline body 3 weight during the intensive phase is associated with reduced mortality.3,4 4 5 There is a paucity of randomized studies that have reported the impact of macronutrient 6 support on weight gain in persons with tuberculosis (PWTB). Indeed, the 2016 COCHRANE 7 review reported only included five underpowered studies that assessed the impact of 8 macronutrient support on weight gain.2,5 Although PWTB in the RATIONS study showed 9 meaningful weight gain, the lack of a control group makes it difficult to discern the impact of 10 nutritional support. Extrapolating weight gain data from studies of general populations is 11 unwise, as TB induces profound metabolic alterations.2 12 13 Here, we present data from an open-label, randomized-controlled trial of an energy-dense 14 nutritional supplement (EDNS) to understand its impact on weight gain during TB treatment. 15 16 Methods: 17 Study Design and Setting 18 We conducted this open-label, two-arm randomized controlled trial between 2020 and 2023 in 19 two tuberculosis (TB) units in Faridabad district, Haryana, India. Ethics committee of All India 20 Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, approved the study (IEC-110/09.03.2018, RP- 21 23/2018, OP-7/2.8.2019). The trial was registered with Central Trial Registry of India 22 (CTRI/2019/12/022574). 23 24 Participants 25 We enrolled adults (≥18 years) with microbiologically confirmed, drug-sensitive pulmonary TB 26 and mild to moderate undernutrition (BMI 14–18.5 kg/m²) receiving treatment under the 27 National TB Elimination Programme (NTEP). We excluded individuals with peanut allergies, 28 pregnancy or lactation, prior diabetes diagnosis or fasting glucose/HbA1c abnormalities, HIV 29 seropositivity, renal or hepatic impairment, or poor general condition. Participants provided 30 written consent, and the. 31 32 Randomization and Blinding 33 We randomized participants to either the intervention or control arm using a computer- 34 generated sequence and ensured allocation concealment with sequentially numbered, opaque, 35 sealed envelopes. Blinding was not feasible for participants or investigators. 36 37 38 Intervention 39 Participants in the intervention arm received a previously described EDNS weekly alongside 40 standard dietary advice. Each 92 g EDNS sachet provided 500 kcal, 13 g protein, 29 g fat, and 41 micronutrients.6 They consumed two sachets daily for six months or until reaching a BMI of 21 42

Both groups received standard 43 TB treatment. 44 45 Outcome Assessments 46 The primary outcomes were 5% weight gain from baseline at two months and 10% at treatment 47 completion. We weighed participants monthly. Secondary outcomes included EDNS 48 acceptability (assessed via a structured questionnaire on taste, smell, consistency, color, and 49 ease of use after one month), adherence (measured by counting returned empty sachets), 50 adverse effects (recorded biweekly), and hemoglobin improvement. 51 52 Data Collection and Management 53 We collected data electronically using the Open Data Kit (ODK) platform on Android devices and 54 securely stored it on a local MySQL server. 55 56 Statistical Analysis 57 We used box plots to compare percent weight gain in the control and intervention groups over 58 six months. Intervention group participants also had higher odds 89 of gaining 10% body weight by month 6 (aOR: 1.89 (95% CI: 1.13-3.18). (Supplementary table 3) 90 91 Secondary outcomes 92 Acceptability and adherence 93 All participants (100%) found the sachet easy to open, though only 76.2% fully understood the 94 instructions. Taste was acceptable to 96.7%, smell to 99.1%, and consistency to 99.9% of 95 participants. Study personnel observed positive facial expressions in 76.2% of instances. 96 Additionally, 89.9% of participants reported subjective health improvements after consuming 97 EDNS. Adherence was high, with an overall rate of 88.7%, with 71% of participants never 98 missing a sachet. 99 100 Adverse Events 101 Nausea and vomiting were more frequent in the intervention group, occurring in 10.2% vs. 4.3% 102 (p = 0.055) and 7.5% vs. 3.6% (p = 0.149) of observed weeks, respectively. Abdominal fullness 103 was also higher (12.9% vs. 5.4%, p = 0.032). Other adverse effects did not significantly differ 104 between groups. (Supplementary table 4) 105 106 Hemoglobin recovery 107 Mean hemoglobin at baseline was 10.8 g/dL (SD 2.0). The hemoglobin gain at 2 months was 0.7 108 g/dL (SD 1.8) in the EDNS arm and 0.5 g/dL (SD 1.6) in the control arm (p=0.315), while at 6 109 months, it was 1.0 g/dL (SD 2.0) in the EDNS arm and 1.1 g/dL (SD 1.7) in the control arm 110 (p=0.830). 111 112 Discussion: 113 To our knowledge, this is the largest randomized controlled trial to assess the impact of 114 macronutrient support using a ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) on weight gain among 115 PWTB. We found that undernourished PWTB receiving EDNS gained more weight. Importantly, a 116 higher proportion of EDNS recipients gained 5% body weight by the end of the intensive phase. 117 This study provides a strong rationale for the use of EDNS to enhance the nutritional recovery of 118 PWTB. 119 120 Notably, the weight gain among EDNS recipients was comparable to that seen among PWTB in 121 the RATIONS study, which provided food baskets with 1200 Kcal per day. The RATIONS study 122 PWTB had a mean baseline BMI of 16.4 (SD: 2.5) which was comparable to that of our 123 participants. At month 2, 53.9% of EDNS recipients gained 5% of their baseline body weight, 124 which was similar to the 54% of PWTB in RATIONS who attained the same metric. At the end of 125 month 6, EDNS recipients had a median 11.7% weight gain (IQR: 6.1-18.1) which is almost 126 identical to the RATIONS study (median 11.6%, IQR: 6.4-17.4). This comparison provides 127 confidence that RUTFs such as EDNS are comparable to food baskets in improving weight gain. 128 129

One significant drawback of food baskets is the uncertainty about PWTB getting an adequate 130 caloric load. Parents may instead prioritize their children’s nutrition, for instance. Gender 131 dynamics may also come into play. Further, time-consuming preparation and fuel poverty may 132 also inhibit the utilization of food baskets. And while Indian PWTB receive cash transfers 133 through the Nikshay Poshan Yojana, the impact of cash transfers on tangible nutritional metrics 134 among PWTB remains uncertain. RUTFs such as EDNS have been vetted in numerous clinical 135 studies for use in contexts such as severe-acute malnutrition.7 Providing a dedicated nutritional 136 supplement to persons with TB may help them attain a suitable caloric load, improving drug 137 absorption, and potentially reducing drug toxicity, relapse, and mortality, particularly if provided 138 promptly at treatment initiation.8 Moreover, the EDNS can be modified to meet the needs of 139 special populations such as those with diabetes. 140 141 This study has several limitations. First, as an open-label trial, the lack of participant and 142 investigator blinding may have introduced biases. Second, the study was conducted in two TB 143 units in Faridabad which may limit generalizability to regions with different socio-economic or 144 cultural contexts. Third, unmeasured factors such as dietary variations outside the intervention 145 or social determinants of health could have influenced the outcomes. Finally, the exclusion of 146 certain high-risk populations, such as those with diabetes or HIV, limits the applicability of our 147 findings to these key and vulnerable subgroups. More research is needed to optimize the 148 composition of EDNS for these populations as well as for children and pregnant women. 149 150 Our study demonstrates that EDNS effectively enhances weight gain among undernourished 151 PWTB while being acceptable and with minimal adverse events, offering a practical and scalable 152 solution for targeted caloric and micronutrient delivery. However, EDNS alone cannot resolve 153 the widespread food insecurity faced by many PWTB. An integrated approach, as proposed by 154 India’s National TB Elimination Program— combining cash transfers, food baskets, and EDNS-- 155 may provide a more comprehensive and sustainable strategy to improve nutritional outcomes 156 and treatment success than any of these strategies. 157

Summary: Undernutrition is the leading cause of tuberculosis in India. Using a Markov state-transition 25

model, we found that food baskets for household contacts of persons with tuberculosis would be cost- 26

effective in reducing tuberculosis incidence and mortality in India. 27

28

Research in context 29

Evidence before this study: Undernutrition is the leading risk factor for TB worldwide. Recently, the 30

RATIONS study demonstrated a roughly 40% reduction in incident TB among household contacts who 31

received in-kind macronutrient and micronutrient supplementation. 32

33

Added value of this study: Although the RATIONS study demonstrated a dramatic reduction in incident 34

TB, it is unclear if nutritional interventions to prevent TB are cost-effective. Previously, only one cost- 35

effectiveness analysis of nutritional interventions for household contacts has been published. Due to lack 36

of published data, that study had to make assumptions regarding the impact of nutritional interventions on 37

TB incidence and mortality. In this study, we conducted an economic evaluation of a RATIONS-style 38

intervention to reduce incident TB and mortality in India using observed data. 39

40

Implications of all the available evidence: In-kind nutritional supplementation for household contacts of 41

individuals with TB disease would be cost-effective in reducing incident TB and TB mortality, 42

particularly if TB programs leverage economies of scale to bring down the cost of the nutritional 43

intervention. 44

ABSTRACT 47

Background: Undernutrition is the leading cause of tuberculosis (TB) globally, but nutritional 48

interventions are often considered cost prohibitive. The RATIONS study demonstrated that nutritional 49

support provided to household contacts of persons with TB can reduce TB incidence. However, the long- 50

term cost-effectiveness of this intervention is unclear. 51

Methods: We assessed the cost-effectiveness of a RATIONS-style intervention (daily 750 kcal dietary 52

supplementation and multi-micronutrient tablet). Using a Markov state transition model we simulated 53

TB incidence, treatment, and TB-attributable mortality among household contacts receiving the 54

RATIONS intervention, as compared to no nutritional support. We calculated health outcomes (TB cases, 55

TB deaths, and disability-adjusted life years [DALYs]) over the lifetime of intervention recipients and 56

assessed costs from government and societal perspectives. We tested the robustness of results to 57

parameter changes via deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analysis. 58

Findings: Over two years, household contacts receiving the RATIONS intervention would experience 39% 59

(95% uncertainty interval (UI): 23–52) fewer TB cases and 59% (95% UI: 44–69) fewer TB deaths. The 60

intervention was estimated to avert 13,775 (95% UI: 9036–20,199) TB DALYs over the lifetime of the 61

study cohort comprising 100,000 household contacts and was cost-effective from both government 62

(incremental cost-effectiveness ratio: $229 per DALY averted [95% UI: 133–387]) and societal 63

perspectives ($184 per DALY averted [95% UI: 83–344]). The results were most sensitive to the cost of 64

the nutritional supplement. 65

Interpretation 66

Prompt nutritional support for household contacts of persons with TB disease would be cost-effective in 67

reducing TB incidence and mortality in India. 68

INTRODUCTION 73

Tuberculosis (TB) has regained its position as the leading infectious cause of death worldwide, with 10.6 74

million cases and 1.3 million deaths in 2022.(1) Undernutrition blunts the innate and adaptive immune 75

response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the pathogen that causes TB.(2) At least 2.2 million of 10.6 76

million TB cases are attributable to undernutrition, making it the leading risk factor for TB.(1) There is 77

also evidence that, among individuals diagnosed with TB disease, undernourished individuals face higher 78

risks of death, treatment failure, and relapse despite undergoing antimycobacterial therapy.(2, 3) 79

Historical data suggest that nutritional supplementation could have a beneficial role by reducing the 80

incidence of TB disease and reducing case fatality among those with TB disease.(2) However, in the 81

absence of contemporary empirical data, nutritional supplementation for persons with TB (PWTB) and 82

their household contacts (HHCs) has not been widely adopted. 83

84

The recently published RATIONS study randomized more than 10,000 household contacts of persons 85

with TB in eastern India between a control arm that received routine TB care with no additional in-kind 86

nutritional supplementation and an intervention arm that received macronutrient and micronutrient 87

support with a food basket that cost $13 per month for 6 months.(4) Compared to the control group, 88

the intervention group experienced a 40% reduction in TB incidence over the following two years. PWTB 89

in the RATIONS study, who also received nutritional support regardless of whether their household 90

contacts were in the control or intervention groups, experienced an approximately 35% reduction in 91

mortality compared to a previous National TB Elimination Program cohort. The RATIONS study shows 92

the potential nutritional supplementation to prevent TB incidence and mortality among household 93

contacts of PWTB. 94

In this study, we developed a Markov state transition model to explore if a RATIONS-style nutritional 96

intervention would be cost-effective for reducing TB incidence and mortality in India. 97

METHODS 98

99

Study Design 100

We used a Markov cohort model to estimate the long-term costs and health outcomes of providing a 101

food basket to HIV-negative household contacts of PWTB in India. We parameterized intervention costs 102

and effect sizes from the results of the RATIONS study, which was conducted among household contacts 103

of PWTB in Jharkhand, India, in a largely rural population with a high degree of multidimensional 104

poverty.(4) We conducted the study from the perspective of India’s central government, which funds 105

the National TB Elimination Program (NTEP). Recognizing that patient costs can often be substantially 106

larger than provider costs, we also conducted a secondary analysis to estimate results from a societal 107

perspective, considering costs borne by both patients and the Indian government. We programmed the 108

model using TreeAge Pro v.22.2.0 (Tree Age, Williamstown, MA). 109

110

Intervention strategies 111

We modeled two strategies. The “usual intervention” strategy reflects the status quo wherein 112

household contacts and PWTB do not receive any in-kind nutritional support. In the RATIONS 113

intervention, HHCs of PWTB receive a food basket that contains a daily multi-micronutrient tablet, rice, 114

and lentils for 6 months.(4) The food basket provides 23g of protein and a total of 750 Kcal calories daily. 115

In addition, under the RATIONS intervention we assumed that individuals progressing to TB disease 116

would receive a nutritional supplement that provided 1200 Kcal with 52g of protein for all six months of 117

TB treatment. 118

Study Model 120

The Markov model simulates the natural course of TB incidence, cure, and sequelae for a starting cohort 121

without TB disease. The model was constructed as a set of mutually exclusive health states, with natural 122

history transitions represented by movements between these health states: development of TB disease, 123

TB cure, death from TB, and death from other causes (Figure 1). Parameters defining TB incidence rates 124

were specified to represent differences in the rates of progression to TB disease based on individual 125

nutritional status. Individuals developing TB disease could die, self-cure, or be cured via treatment. 126

Individuals who survive TB transition to an early post-treatment state, where they have an elevated risk 127

of recurrent disease for 12 months as well as increased all-cause mortality. Following 12 months in the 128

early-post treatment phase, individuals transition to the late post-treatment phase, where they continue 129

to have increased all-cause mortality, but where their risk of TB disease falls to baseline. We assumed 130

that after surviving TB, individuals would have a lower average quality of life due to chronic post-TB lung 131

disease. We used the model to simulate progression of a cohort of 100,000 household contacts of PWTB 132

through these health states over their lifetime, with a 6-month time step. 133

Outcomes from the simulation included TB disease incidence, TB deaths, disability-adjusted life years 138

(DALYs), and costs from the government perspective. In a secondary analysis, we also considered costs 139

from a societal perspective. All outcomes were assessed over the lifetime of the modelled cohort. 140

Intervention impact 159

We assumed that prompt nutritional supplementation would reduce the risk of incident TB disease 160

among HHCs. Based on the results of the RATIONS study, we assumed an incidence rate ratio of 0·61 161

(95% CI 0·43, 0·85) for HHCs receiving supplementation compared to no supplementation for two years 162

from the beginning of the intervention. After two years, we assumed that those receiving the 163

intervention and those receiving usual care had a similar risk of incident TB disease. We assumed that 164

PWTB who receive nutritional support have reduced TB-related mortality based on a comparison of 165

outcomes of PWTB in the RATIONS study to an NTEP cohort, operationalized as a risk ratio of 0·65 (95% 166

CI: 0·49, 0·85) applied between TB incidence and cure.(6, 11) 167

We used cost data from the RATIONS study, which reported supplementation costs of $13 per month 169

inclusive of delivery costs. In sensitivity analyses, we examined a wide range of values for the cost of the 170

nutritional supplementation, to account for regional variation, diversion of food grains, and wastage. We 171

obtained TB treatment costs from a recent published study.(12) For costs borne by TB patients and 172

affected households, we assumed that the direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, and 173

productivity losses borne by TB-affected household would be $700 (SD: 140) per TB episode.(13, 14) We 174

rounded all costs to the nearest dollar. All costs are reported in 2022 US dollars. 175

176

Cost-effectiveness analysis 177

We employed the model to compare the RATIONS nutritional supplementation intervention to the 178

status quo. We projected TB cases, TB deaths, disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) attributable to TB, 179

and costs for each strategy over the lifetime of the study cohort. We calculated incremental cost- 180

effectiveness ratios (ICERs) as the ratio of mean incremental costs to mean incremental health benefits, 181

for the intervention compared to the usual care strategy. Costs and DALYs were discounted at 3% per 182

annum.(15) 183

184

Willingness-to-pay 185

We derived our willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold from Ochalek et al., who estimated country-specific 186

willingness-to-pay thresholds based on the opportunity cost of healthcare spending.(16) For India, this 187

study estimated a WTP threshold equivalent to 23% of per-capita GDP (US$550 in 2022). We considered 188

ICERs below this threshold to be clearly cost-effective. 189

To assess the robustness of our results, we conducted both deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity 192

analyses.(17) For the deterministic sensitivity analysis, we defined a priori feasible ranges around core 193

parameter values (Table 1) and then repeated the analysis multiple times, each time varying one 194

parameter between the maximum and minimum of the feasible range, with other parameters held at 195

their point estimate. Next, we conducted two-way sensitivity analyses, in which we simultaneously 196

varied the parameters that emerged as the most important from one-way sensitivity analyses. 197

198

Lastly, we performed probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA). We defined uncertainty in parameter values 199

as probability density functions (PDFs) for each model parameter. We then employed 2nd-order Monte 200

Carlo simulation to repeat the analysis 10,000 times, each time drawing a random value for each model 201

parameter from its PDF. This produced 10,000 estimates for each model outcomes, with the distribution 202

of these estimates quantifying the uncertainty in model outcomes due to the combined uncertainty 203

from all model parameters. We report the PSA results using cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.(18) 204

In addition, we report uncertainty around main analysis results using 95% uncertainty intervals 205

calculated from the PSA results. 206

Sensitivity analysis 239

One-way sensitivity analyses for the general population showed that the two parameters with the 240

greatest impact on the ICER were the pre-recipient cost of the RATIONS supplementation (baseline 241

assumption: $28.5, range: $20-100) and the risk ratio of TB incidence for those receiving the nutritional 242

supplementation (baseline assumption: 0.61, range: 0.43 to 0.85) (Table 4). In threshold analyses, the 243

cost-effectiveness ratio for the RATIONS intervention was below to the WTP threshold ($550 per DALY 244

averted) when the cost of supplementation was less than $75, indicating that the intervention would be 245

cost-effective for any supplementation cost below this value. Even when we assumed the risk ratio for 246

TB incidence was 0.99, the WTP threshold was not exceeded. The model was less sensitive to the risk 247

reduction in TB mortality, the cost of TB treatment, and the disability weight for post-TB lung disease 248

(Table 4). 249

In two-way sensitivity analyses, the RATIONS intervention was cost-effective across a large range of 250

costs of the supplement and risk ratio of TB incidence (Figure 3). When the cost of the supplement for 251

HHCs was below $56, the intervention was always cost-effective from the government perspective. 252

When considering the societal perspective, the intervention remained below the WTP threshold as long 253

as the supplementation cost was below $59. We also conducted a two-way sensitivity analysis of the risk 254

ratios for TB incidence and TB mortality. Even at the lowest estimates of the risk ratio for TB incidence 255

(0.85) and TB mortality (0.85), the RATIONS intervention remained cost-effective with an ICER of $514. 256

257

Lastly, in probabilistic sensitivity analysis, the RATIONS intervention was favored at a WTP of $550 in 258

99.95% and 99.97% of model simulations from both the government and societal perspectives, 259

respectively. Indeed, RATIONS was consistently preferable in >99% of iterations at a WTP of $440. From 260

a societal perspective RATIONS was consistently favorable in >99% of iterations at a WTP of $396. Cost 261

DISCUSSION 265

Nutritional interventions to mitigate risks of TB incidence and mortality are often perceived to be cost 266

prohibitive. However, the RATIONS study has provided empirical evidence that low-cost nutritional 267

support could have a substantial impact on lowering the risk of incident TB in settings with high rates of 268

multidimensional poverty and undernutrition. Our analysis suggests that an in-kind nutritional 269

intervention modelled on the food basket used in the RATIONS study could be cost-effective for 270

reducing TB incidence and mortality in India. We estimated that RATIONS-style nutritional support 271

would have a cost-effectiveness of $229 per DALY averted from a healthcare perspective and $184 per 272

DALY averted from a societal perspective. Our findings can help national TB programs as they consider 273

the economics of implementing nutritional support to reduce the incidence of TB among household 274

contacts. 275

276

Balanced nutritional interventions likely reduce incident TB disease by enhancing the humoral and 277

innate responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis; these responses can help infected individuals 278

eliminate or contain the bacilli.(2) Nutritional support to malnourished individuals may acutely restore 279

their immune response. Indeed, mouse models suggest that providing a protein-rich diet to protein- 280

deficient mice can restore their anti-tubercular immune response within two weeks.(19) Given that the 281

majority of TB disease in high burden settings arises from infection within the past two years, nutritional 282

support should be provided to HHCs promptly after the diagnosis of the index case to prevent incident 283

TB disease.(20) 284

In our model, we limited the reduction in TB incidence among HHCs to two years after exposure since 286

this was the duration of follow-up observed in the RATIONS study. For subsequent years, we assumed 287

that individuals receiving the RATIONS intervention would have the same incidence rate as the usual 288

care group, which remained elevated in years 3, 4, and 5 since exposure. Given the impact of nutritional 289

support on the immune response to TB, it is possible that individuals receiving improved nutrition are 290

more resistant to new TB infection. If so, the incidence reductions produced by the RATIONS 291

intervention could extend beyond the two years assumed in this analysis. As such, our health impact and 292

cost-effectiveness estimates may be conservative. 293

294

It is important to note that that the RATIONS study—on which this cost-effectiveness analysis was 295

based—was conducted in a population with high levels of material deprivation and undernutrition, and 296

TB incidence rates higher than those estimated for other parts of India. It is possible that the impact and 297

cost-effectiveness of nutritional support may be lower in settings with a lower prevalence and severity 298

of undernutrition, or lower TB incidence. Our two-way sensitivity analysis suggests that even at the 299

lowest estimates of risk reduction for TB incidence (15% reduction) and mortality (15% reduction), the 300

intervention would remain below the WTP threshold. These are credible effect sizes in less 301

impoverished populations. A systematic review, which largely drew on data from high income countries, 302

found a log-linear relationship between BMI and TB incidence wherein TB incidence decreases by 303

approximately 14% per 1kg/m2 increase in BMI which is entirely achievable in 6 months on the RATIONS 304

intervention. Further, a systematic review of randomized trials of macronutrient supplementation in 305

PWTB, despite being underpowered, estimated that macronutrient supplementation was associated 306

with a RR of 0.34 (95% CI: 0.10–1.20) for TB mortality.(21) 307

Public health investments to eliminate TB and undernutrition have historically provided some of the 309

greatest returns on investment.(22, 23) The ICER estimated for nutritional support in our study is 310

considerably below both the country-specific WTP threshold for India and the ICER for well-accepted TB 311

preventive interventions, such as test-driven isoniazid preventive therapy for persons with HIV/AIDS 312

($1154 per DALY averted).(24) In our model, the ICER was most sensitive to the cost of nutritional 313

supplementation for HHCs. Even when we assumed the lowest possible effect of nutritional 314

interventions on incident TB disease, nutritional support would be cost-effective at $56 per recipient 315

over 6 months, which was nearly twice the cost of the intervention. It is possible that state and national 316

governments would enjoy economies of scale, not possible in the context of a clinical trial, that 317

consequently could further lower the cost of the intervention. 318

319

Our analysis has several limitations. First, we did not model the impact of nutritional interventions on 320

reducing early relapses and disengagement from care, even though these are plausible effects.(2, 25) 321

Second, we did not account for reductions in TB transmission and secondary TB cases that might result 322

from lower TB incidence, and instead focused on the direct health benefits experienced by intervention 323

recipients. Third, our cost assumptions were limited to drug-susceptible TB, which is less costly to treat 324

than drug-resistant TB, (13) and we also did not model the medical and non-medical costs faced by 325

PWTB prior to their diagnosis. Approximately two-thirds of Indian PWTB treated in the public sector first 326

seek care in the private sector and accrue large costs before an accurate TB diagnosis is made.(13) Forth, 327

the model did not capture the positive externalities of nutritional support, including improvements in 328

nutritional status and functional recovery and improved economic productivity among TB survivors, 329

which have been explored in a previous analysis.(26) Taken together, these limitations suggest that our 330

ICER estimates will be conservative, and that nutritional support could be even more cost-effective than 331

we project. 332

Improvements in population-level nutrition and progress on social determinants of health likely 334

contributed to the massive decline in TB incidence and mortality in countries like the United States and 335

the United Kingdom that occurred even prior to the introduction of antimicrobials.(25) The striking 336

findings of the RATIONS study have demonstrated the role nutritional interventions can play in the 337

contemporary era to accelerate TB elimination. India is well positioned to institute a large-scale 338

nutritional support program as it already has well-established infrastructure for delivering in-kind 339

rations, mid-day meals, and nutritional counseling.(27-29) The TB Mitra Program, which crowdsources 340

nutritional support for persons with TB, could also be scaled up.(30) 341

342

Additional research is necessary to help us understand how to target nutritional interventions equitably 343

and efficiently. Operational studies are needed to design optimal delivery systems. Even as nutritional 344

interventions are operationalized in settings with lower prevalence of undernutrition in India, 345

epidemiological studies can help us understand the effect size of nutritional interventions in diverse 346

populations. We also need clinical and translational studies to better define the nutritional needs of 347

special populations, such as pregnant women and children, to develop the best possible nutritional 348

package. Economic evaluations should be conducted alongside nutritional intervention studies to inform 349

policy. 350

351

In conclusion, our analysis projected that a RATIONS-style intervention would be cost-effective for 352

populations with a high dual burden of TB and undernutrition in India and drive large reductions in TB 353

incidence and mortality among household contacts of persons with TB. 354

# In-kind nutritional supplementation for persons with drug-susceptible tuberculosis and their household contacts would be cost-effective for reducing tuberculosis incidence and mortality in Jharkhand, India: a modeling study

**Authors:** Pranay Sinha; Madhavi Bhargava; Madolyn Dauphinais; Madeline E. Carwile; C. Robert Horsburgh; Urvashi B. Singh; Sonali Sarkar; Anurag Bhargava; Nicolas A. Menzies

**Affiliations:** 1.Section of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine, MA, USA | 2.Boston Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 3.Department of Community Medicine, Yenepoya Medical College, Mangalore, India | 4.Center for Nutrition Studies, Yenepoya (Deemed to be University), Mangalore, India | 5.Department of Epidemiology, Boston University School of Public Health, MA, USA | 6.Department of Microbiology, All India Institute of Medical Sciences, New Delhi, India | 7.National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme, New Delhi, India | 8.Department of Preventive and Social Medicine, Jawaharlal Institute of Postgraduate Medical Education and Research, Puducherry, India | 9.Department of Medicine, Yenepoya Medical College, Mangalore, India | 10.Department of Medicine, Kasturba Medical College Mangalore | 11.Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, Karnataka, India | 12.Department of Medicine, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada | 13.Center for Health Decision Sciences, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA | 14.Department of Global Health and Population, Harvard TH Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

Undernutrition is the leading cause of tuberculosis (TB) globally, but nutritional interventions are often considered cost-prohibitive. The RATIONS study demonstrated that nutritional supplementation to household contacts of persons with TB can reduce TB incidence, yet economic evaluations of such strategies remain limited.

Using a Markov model, we assessed the cost-effectiveness of a RATIONS-style intervention (monthly food basket providing 750 kcal, 23g of protein, and a multi-micronutrient tablet daily) for household contacts of persons with TB, as compared to no nutritional support. We calculated health outcomes (TB episodes, TB deaths, and disability-adjusted life years [DALYs]) over the lifetime of intervention recipients and assessed costs from healthcare and societal perspectives. We tested the robustness of results to parameter changes via deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analysis.

Over two years, household contacts receiving the RATIONS intervention experienced 38% (95% uncertainty interval [UI]: 23–52) fewer TB episodes and 58% (95% UI: 44–70) fewer TB deaths. Over the lifetime of a cohort of 100,000 household contacts, the intervention was projected to avert 11,524 DALYs (95% UI: 7,446–17,393) and was cost-effective from both the healthcare (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio [ICER]: $289 per DALY averted [95% UI: 156–537]) and societal perspectives ($229 per DALY averted [95% UI: 102–468]). Cost-effectiveness was most sensitive to the cost of the nutritional supplement.

Prompt nutritional support for household contacts of persons with TB disease would be cost-effective in reducing TB incidence and mortality in India.

## INTRODUCTION

Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading infectious cause of death worldwide, with 10.8 million persons experiencing TB disease and 1.25 million TB deaths in 2023.(1) Undernutrition weakens the immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is the leading risk factor for TB globally.(2) Undernourished PWTB face higher risks of death, treatment failure, and relapse despite undergoing antimycobacterial therapy.(2, 3)

The RATIONS (Reducing Activation of Tuberculosis by Improvement of Nutritional Status) study randomized more than 10,000 household contacts (HHCs) of persons with tuberculosis (PWTB) in the Indian state of Jharkhand between a control arm that received routine TB care with no additional in-kind nutritional supplementation and an intervention arm that received macronutrient and micronutrient support with an inexpensive food basket for six months.(4) PWTB in both arms received nutritional support. Compared to the control group, the intervention group experienced a nearly 40% reduction in TB incidence over the following two years. PWTB in the RATIONS study, who also received nutritional support regardless of whether their HHCs were in the control or intervention groups, experienced an approximately 35% reduction in mortality compared to a previous National TB Elimination Program (NTEP) cohort.(5)

We developed a Markov state transition model to explore if a RATIONS-style nutritional intervention would be cost-effective for reducing TB incidence and mortality in Jharkhand.

## METHODS

### Study Design

We developed a Markov cohort model to estimate the long-term costs and health outcomes of providing a food basket to HHCs of PWTB in India, following current best-practice guidelines for cost-effectiveness modelling.(6, 7) We parameterized intervention costs and effect sizes from the results of the RATIONS study, which was conducted among HHCs of PWTB in Jharkhand, India, in a largely rural population with a high degree of multidimensional poverty.(4) We conducted the study from the healthcare perspective. Recognizing that societal costs can often be substantially higher than provider costs, we also conducted a secondary analysis to estimate results from a societal perspective, considering costs borne by both PWTB and the Indian government which funds the NTEP. We programmed the model using TreeAge Pro v.22.2.0 (Tree Age, Williamstown, MA).

### Model Population

Our modeled population resembled the HHC cohort enrolled in the RATIONS study conducted in Jharkhand, India. Full details of this population have been described elsewhere, but briefly: the median age was 21.5 years (IQR: 11.0–36.8), and undernutrition was highly prevalent—38.3% of individuals receiving nutritional support met age-appropriate criteria for undernutrition.(4) Only 0.15% were living with HIV. These values informed our model assumptions regarding baseline nutritional status and age structure in the HHC population.

### Intervention strategies

We modeled two strategies. The “usual intervention” strategy reflects the status quo, wherein HHCs and PWTB do not receive any in-kind nutritional support. In the RATIONS intervention, PWTB received a nutritional supplement that provided 1200 Kcal with 52g of protein for all six months of TB treatment.(4) HHCs of PWTB receive a food basket containing a daily multi-micronutrient tablet, rice, and lentils that provide 23g of protein and a total of 750 Kcal daily.

### Study Model

The Markov model was designed to simulate the natural course of TB incidence, treatment, and long-term sequelae for a starting cohort without TB disease. It comprised a set of mutually exclusive health states in six-month time steps: development of TB disease, TB cure, death from TB, and death from other causes (Figure 1).

Importantly, TB disease was modeled as a transition event rather than a persistent health state. Individuals who developed TB disease either died within the same time step (based on fatality rate assumptions) or were assumed to be diagnosed and cured—either through treatment or spontaneous recovery—and then entered the early post-treatment state. This structure allowed the model to explicitly capture TB incidence, recurrence, and TB-related mortality, while maintaining parsimony.

Individuals who survived TB entered the early post-treatment state, where they experienced elevated risk of recurrent TB and increased all-cause mortality for 12 months. After this period, they transitioned to the late post-treatment state, where recurrence risk returned to baseline but excess mortality persisted. We assumed that all TB survivors had reduced quality of life due to chronic post-TB lung disease. The model simulated the lifetime trajectory of a cohort of 100,000 HHCs of persons with TB (PWTB) across these health states.

### Parameter Inputs

#### Health Outcomes

Outcomes of interest from the simulation included TB disease incidence, TB deaths, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), and costs from the healthcare perspective. In a secondary analysis, we also considered costs from a societal perspective. All outcomes were assessed over the lifetime of the modeled cohort.

We sourced TB incidence rates for HHCs after exposure from a previous meta-analysis.(8) Table 1 presents incidence estimates adopted for the analysis for the first five years. After five years of elevated risk of TB disease, we assumed the incidence would drop to prevailing rates in Jharkhand: 130/100,000 as reported in the RATIONS study.(4) Given that substate variations are possible, we conducted sensitivity analysis with a lower incidence of 65/100,000 and a higher incidence of 390/100,000 as well. To account for the long-term secular declines in the incidence of TB in the population, we assumed a 3% annual decline based on incidence trends estimated for India over the past five years based on data from the WHO global TB report (1) (Supplementary table 1). In the early post-treatment phase, we assumed that TB survivors had an increased risk of recurrent TB based on observed data from India.(5) In the late post-treatment phase, the risk dropped to baseline.

We obtained TB fatality rates from the WHO Global TB Report 2022.(3) Using WHO life tables for background mortality rates, we constructed TB-deleted life tables.(9) For individuals surviving TB, we estimated a lifetime increase in TB-attributable mortality using previous conservative estimates.(10)

To calculate DALYs, we applied an annual disability weight of 0.333 (95% CI: 0.224–0.454), based on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019, for 6 months to represent the symptomatic phase of TB disease, and a disability weight of 0.053 (95% CI: 0.026–0.079), from Quaife et al. (2020), for the remainder of life expectancy among those cured of TB.(11, 12)

#### Intervention impact

We assumed prompt nutritional supplementation would reduce the risk of incident TB disease among HHCs. Based on the results of the RATIONS study, we assumed an incidence rate ratio of 0·61 (95% CI 0·43, 0·85) for HHCs receiving supplementation compared to no supplementation for two years from the beginning of the intervention. After two years, we assumed that those receiving the intervention and those receiving usual care had a similar risk of incident TB disease. If HHCs developed TB disease during the model horizon, we assumed they would then receive nutritional support PWTB, which would reduce TB-related mortality. This mortality benefit was based on a comparison of outcomes of PWTB in the RATIONS study to an NTEP cohort, which yielded a risk ratio (RR) of 0·65 (95% CI: 0·49, 0·85).(5, 13) We did not model the mortality benefit for the index PWTB.

We used cost data from the RATIONS study, which reported supplementation costs of $14.7 per month, including delivery costs for PWTB and $4.75 per month for each HHC. In sensitivity analyses, we examined a wide range of values for the cost of nutritional supplementation to account for regional variation, diversion of food grains, and wastage. We obtained TB treatment costs from a microcosting study.(14) For costs borne by PWTB and affected households, we assumed that the direct medical costs, direct non-medical costs, and productivity losses borne by TB-affected households would be $700 (SD: 140) per TB episode.(15, 16) We rounded all costs to the nearest dollar. All costs are reported in 2024 US dollars.

### Cost-effectiveness analysis

We calculated incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) as the ratio of mean incremental costs to mean incremental health benefits (DALYs averted) for the intervention compared to the usual care strategy. Costs and DALYs were discounted at 3% per annum.(17)

#### Willingness-to-pay

We derived our willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold from Ochalek et al., who estimated country-specific willingness-to-pay thresholds based on the opportunity cost of healthcare spending.(18) For India, this study estimated a WTP threshold equivalent to 23% of per-capita GDP (US$570 in 2024). We considered ICERs below this threshold to be cost-effective.

### Sensitivity analysis

To assess the robustness of our results, we conducted both deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses.(19) For the deterministic sensitivity analysis, we defined a priori feasible ranges around core parameter values (Table 1). Then, we repeated the analysis multiple times, each time varying one parameter between the maximum and minimum of the feasible range, with other parameters held at their point estimate. Next, we conducted two-way sensitivity analyses, in which we simultaneously varied the parameters that emerged as the most important from one-way sensitivity analyses.

Lastly, we performed probabilistic sensitivity analysis (PSA). We defined uncertainty in parameter values as probability density functions (PDFs) for each model parameter. We then employed 2nd-order Monte Carlo simulation to repeat the analysis 10,000 times, each time drawing a random value for each model parameter from its PDF. This produced 10,000 estimates for each model outcome, with the distribution of these estimates quantifying the uncertainty in model outcomes due to the combined uncertainty from all model parameters. We report the PSA results using cost-effectiveness acceptability curves.(20) In addition, we report uncertainty around the main analysis results using equal-tailed 95% uncertainty intervals (UI) calculated from the PSA results.

## RESULTS

### Primary model results

Primary model results are presented in Table 2. Per 100,000 HHCs, those receiving the RATIONS intervention experienced fewer cumulative TB episodes (6958 vs. 7882) and TB-related deaths (651 vs. 1097) over their lifetime, corresponding to 924 TB episodes and 446 TB deaths averted. These differences reflect a risk ratio (RR) of 0.88 (95% UI: 0.83–0.93) for TB incidence and 0.59 (95% UI: 0.49–0.71) for TB mortality. In the first two years of this model, there were 1634 TB episodes (95% UI: 1069–2450) in the RATIONS intervention as opposed to 2594 TB episodes (95% UI: 1913–3651) with usual care, RR 0.62 (0.48–0.77). These results are consistent with the empirical findings of the RATIONS trial. The RATIONS intervention averted 11,524 DALYs per 100,000 individuals compared to usual care, with most of the health gains attributable to reductions in TB mortality (Table 3).

From the healthcare perspective, total discounted costs per 100,000 individuals were $0.84 million (95% UI: 0.52–1.41) under usual care—reflecting TB treatment costs—and $4.24 million (95% UI: 3.07–5.64) under the RATIONS intervention, of which $0.72 million (95% UI: 0.44–1.23) was for TB care and the remainder for nutritional support. From the societal perspective, total costs were $5.72 million (95% UI: 3.86–9.23) for the usual care strategy. Total societal costs under the RATIONS intervention were $8.45 million (95% UI: 6.72–12.04).

Compared to the status quo, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of the RATIONS intervention was $289 per DALY averted (95% UI: 156–537) under the healthcare perspective and $229 (95% UI: 102–468) under the societal perspective. Both estimates are below the country-specific WTP threshold of $570 per DALY averted.

### Sensitivity analysis

One-way sensitivity analyses showed that the parameter with the greatest impact on the ICER was the six-month cost of nutritional support for HHCs, with ICERs ranging from $204 to $652 across the tested range ($20–$75). In threshold analysis, the RATIONS intervention remained cost-effective below the WTP when the monthly cost for HHCs was under $65. TB incidence also had a substantial effect, with ICERs ranging from $186 to $436 across the tested range. However, this was largely driven by the variation in the incidence rate in the first 5 years. When we held this period constant and only varied the incidence in the subsequent period between 65 and 390/100,000, the ICER range reduced to $248 to $302. The model was moderately sensitive to the age of the cohort and the protective effect of nutritional support on TB mortality. On threshold analysis, the WTP was met at the risk ratio for mortality of 0.98 (Supplementary figure 1). The effect of nutritional support on TB incidence had a smaller influence on the ICER, which ranged from $238 to $392 across the tested values. Other parameters—including the cost of nutritional support for PWTB, the probability of TB recurrence, the cost of TB treatment, the disability weight for post-TB lung disease, and the increased risk of post-TB mortality—had limited effects on the ICER (Table 4).

In two-way sensitivity analyses (Figure 2), the RATIONS intervention was cost-effective from the healthcare perspective, even at the lowest estimate of TB mortality reduction (RR: 0.85), as long as the six-month supplement cost per HHC did not exceed $44.2. Similarly, when assuming the lowest decrease in TB incidence (RR: 0.85), the RATIONS intervention remained below the WTP threshold at costs below $47. When considering the societal perspective, the corresponding values were $52 and $55. We conducted a two-way sensitivity analysis varying the risk ratios for TB mortality and TB incidence. The RATIONS intervention was the preferred strategy across nearly the entire parameter space, with usual care favored only when the RR of mortality exceeded 0.83 and the RR of incidence exceeded 0.78 (Figure 2b). When considering the societal perspective, the corresponding values were 0.82 and 0.81.

Lastly, in probabilistic sensitivity analysis, the RATIONS intervention was favored at a WTP of $570 in 98.5% and 99.5% of model simulations from the healthcare and societal perspectives, respectively (Figure 3). RATIONS was consistently preferable in >99% of iterations at a WTP of $598 and $530 from these perspectives, respectively.

## DISCUSSION

Nutritional interventions are often perceived to be cost-prohibitive. However, the RATIONS study has provided empirical evidence that low-cost nutritional support for HHCs of individuals diagnosed with TB could have a substantial impact on lowering the risk of incident TB in settings with high rates of multidimensional poverty and undernutrition. Our analysis suggests that an in-kind nutritional intervention modeled after the RATIONS study food basket could be cost-effective for reducing TB incidence and mortality in India, with a cost-effectiveness of $289 per DALY averted from a healthcare perspective and $229 per DALY averted from a societal perspective, when compared to no nutritional support. Our findings can help the NTEP consider the economics of implementing nutritional support to reduce the incidence of TB among HHCs.

In our analysis, the ICER was most sensitive to the cost of nutritional supplementation for HHCs. Even when we assumed the lowest possible effect of dietary interventions on incident TB disease, nutritional support would be cost-effective at $47 per recipient over six months, which is far higher than the reported cost of the intervention during the study. State and national governments are likely to enjoy economies of scale that could further lower the cost of the intervention.

While the RATIONS trial provided nutritional support to all PWTB in both arms, it was not designed to estimate the impact of nutrition on treatment outcomes among PWTB. To approximate this effect, we compared TB-related mortality in the RATIONS cohort to that observed in a cohort from the National TB Elimination Program in similar districts, yielding a risk ratio of 0.65 (95% CI: 0.49–0.85).(5) We acknowledge this is an indirect comparison that may be influenced by differences in implementation context and care quality and that causal inference is challenging. We therefore conducted sensitivity analyses varying this parameter across a wide range, including conservative estimates approaching no mortality benefit, to ensure our conclusions were robust. The ICER remained below the WTP threshold even when the relative reduction in mortality was assumed to be just 2%. Comparison to other evidence suggests the effect sizes we examined in these sensitivity analyses are credible. Indeed, despite being underpowered, a COCHRANE review of macronutrient supplementation estimated that macronutrient supplementation was associated with an RR of 0.34 (95% CI: 0.10–1.20) for TB mortality.(21) As nutritional interventions are scaled up programmatically, there may be opportunities to embed cluster-randomized studies that rigorously assess the impact of nutritional support on TB mortality.

Our analysis has several limitations. The effect parameters were drawn from a single study and may not be representative of India or even the entire state of Jharkhand, as noted above. We did not model the impact of nutritional interventions on treatment failure or loss to follow-up, even though these are plausible effects.(22) Additionally, our model does not explicitly capture potential benefits from intensified household visits under the nutritional support intervention, such as earlier TB detection and treatment initiation or improved adherence, which may further improve health outcomes. This Markov model focused on direct health benefits, but could not account for reductions in TB transmission and secondary TB episodes, but another model suggests that these would be reduced as well.(23) Further, we limited the reduction in TB incidence among HHCs to two years after exposure to match the duration of follow-up observed in the RATIONS study, making our estimates conservative. Our cost assumptions were limited to drug-susceptible TB, which is less costly to treat than drug-resistant TB.(15) Lastly, the model did not capture additional benefits of nutritional support on health and economic productivity.(24)

Public health investments to eliminate TB and undernutrition have historically provided some of the greatest returns on investment.(25, 26) Improvements in population-level nutrition and progress on social determinants of health likely contributed to the massive decline in TB incidence and mortality in the global North before the advent of antimicrobials.(27) India is well-positioned to institute a large-scale nutritional support program as it already has well-established infrastructure for delivering in-kind rations, mid-day meals, and nutritional counseling.(28–30) There are already plans to expand in-kind support through the Nikshay Mitra Program.(31)

In conclusion, our analysis projected that a RATIONS-style intervention would be cost-effective for populations with a high dual burden of TB and undernutrition in India and could drive large reductions in TB incidence and mortality among HHCs of PWTB.

## Abstract

Background Current efforts to reduce global tuberculosis incidence have proved insufficient, highlighting that urgent action is needed to address underlying modifiable risk factors such as undernutrition. We aimed to estimate the global impact of eliminating undernutrition on tuberculosis incidence among adults accounting for varying nutritional status by country, sex, and age, in addition to incorporating the continuous, non-linear relationship between body mass index (BMI) and tuberculosis risk. Methods We used a continuous risk framework to consider the population-level implications of BMI distributions for tuberculosis incidence for those aged ≥15 years. We generated BMI distributions for each country, sex, and age group applying a bilinear model for the logarithmic relative risk of tuberculosis incidence at different BMI values. We assessed the impact of eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition (BMI<17kg/m2) or all undernutrition (BMI<18.5kg/m2) on tuberculosis incidence by constructing counterfactual BMI distributions that redistributed those with low BMI to higher BMI, proportional to the remaining density. Findings We estimated that eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition would avert 1.4 million (95%UI, 1.1-1.7) tuberculosis episodes globally, representing 16.8% (14.3-19.2) of global adult incidence, while eliminating all undernutrition would avert 2.3 million (1.8-2.7) episodes, a reduction of 26.5% (23.2- 29.8). The largest proportional reductions in tuberculosis incidence could be achieved by eliminating undernutrition in the African, South-East Asian, and Eastern Mediterranean regions; females; and adolescent or elderly adults. Interpretation Over a quarter of global tuberculosis incidence in adults would be averted by eliminating undernutrition, approximately three times higher than current estimates. These findings highlight the urgent need to scale up population-level nutritional interventions, which may have myriad social and health benefits beyond tuberculosis, alongside research to determine optimal implementation strategies and impacts. ## Introduction

Tuberculosis is the world’s leading cause of death from a single infection, affecting an estimated 10.8 million people in 2023, and killing 1.25 million.1 Global tuberculosis incidence declined by 8.3% between 2015 and 2023, far short of World Health Organization (WHO) ‘End TB Strategy’ targets of 50% by 2025 and 90% by 2035.1,2 Although the pace of decline has been partly slowed by the impact of COVID- 19,3 clearly these targets are unlikely to be achieved without substantial changes in the epidemic, and in our response.4 While it remains important to improve the effectiveness and coverage of the biomedical interventions underpinning tuberculosis prevention, diagnosis, and treatment, it is also critical to recognise that the global tuberculosis epidemic is driven by multiple modifiable, socially-determined risk factors that could be addressed to reduce tuberculosis incidence.5,6 Undernutrition, which encompasses multiple forms of nutrient deficiency, but is commonly defined in adults by an underweight body mass index (BMI<18.5kg/m2), is one such risk factor. Having undernutrition increases both the risk of developing tuberculosis, and the risk of adverse outcomes once diagnosed and treated.7 Importantly, undernutrition has been shown to be a highly modifiable risk factor both historically and in contemporary contexts. Improved nutrition was a major contributor to the decline in tuberculosis incidence observed in high-income countries during the 20th century;8 and the recent RATIONS study in India demonstrated that providing nutritional support to members of tuberculosisaffected households could reduce tuberculosis incidence by approximately 40%.9 Subsequent modelling estimated a meaningful population-level impact of this intervention on tuberculosis incidence if scaled up to other tuberculosis-affected households nationally, and showed it would be highly likely to be costeffective.10 Given rising food insecurity globally,11 there is a clear need to explore the potential of expanding nutritional interventions beyond tuberculosis-affected households to broader populations with high undernutrition prevalence. To inform health programming, budgeting, and intervention prioritisation, it is important to understand how much tuberculosis incidence could be averted by eliminating undernutrition. To facilitate this, the WHO calculates annual estimates of the number of tuberculosis episodes caused by undernutrition (alongside other risk factors) for each country, based on population attributable fractions (PAF).1 The most recent global PAF estimate of 8.9% was informed by a recent Cochrane review, which estimated the relative risk of tuberculosis in a binary comparison of people with undernutrition (BMI<18.5kg/m2) versus those without undernutrition (BMI≥18.5kg/m2).12 However, because of the established doseresponse relationship between BMI and tuberculosis risk, this binary conceptualisation of a naturally continuous exposure likely underestimates the relative risk and hence the PAF.13,14 Furthermore, given that BMI distributions vary by age, sex, and between and within regions, more granular estimates would enable more targeted and effective policy decisions. A recent systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis has provided updated estimates of how tuberculosis risk changes across the entire BMI range in adults.15 This review showed that tuberculosis risk is highest at the lowest BMI values and decreases non-linearly as BMI increases, with the steepest reductions in tuberculosis risk occurring when moving through underweight and normal weight ranges,

## Methods

We used a continuous risk framework to consider the population-level implications of BMI distributions for tuberculosis incidence by country, sex, and age group for those aged 15 years or older in 2023. An overview of the methods is shown in Figure 1. We focussed on adults because different anthropometric indicators are used in children, and there is limited evidence available on how these indicators influence tuberculosis risk. Ethical approval was not required as this study used only published, aggregate data.

## BMI distributions

We used estimates from the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration (NCD-RisC) for their most recent year (2022) to fit BMI distributions for each country, sex, and 5-year age group.16 We chose gamma distributions based on computational advantages and comparable fit with log-normal distributions on an individual-level BMI test dataset from Peru (Appendix p4). We fitted gamma distributions to their adult (20+ years) estimates by minimizing a sum-of-squares loss function that measured the difference between the population fraction in each of eight BMI ranges, for each country, sex, and age group (Appendix pp5-6), weighted by their precision. Where fitting did not converge, we assigned the distribution for the same sex and country in the age group below. For adolescent (15-19 years) estimates, we used WHO reference BMI tables to convert the z-scores used to define reported categories into absolute BMI values, using the midpoint of the single year age categories in the reference tables. We then minimized a sum-of-squares loss function that measured the difference between the population fraction in each of five BMI ranges, for each country, sex, and singleyear age group (Appendix p5), weighted by their precision. Finally, we constructed an average gamma distribution for the 15-19 year age group to match the means of the single-year gamma distribution means and variances. Where fits of single-year BMI distributions did not converge, these were dropped from this averaging procedure. Normal approximations to the loss function around the optima were used to represent uncertainty in BMI distribution parameters as bivariate normal distributions.

## Relative risks of tuberculosis and counterfactual comparisons

We used a bilinear model for the logarithmic relative risk of tuberculosis incidence at different BMI values, based on the recent systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of Saunders et al. (see right graph in Figure 1).15 Relative risks of tuberculosis incidence comparing populations were computed by taking the ratio of mean relative risks over each population’s BMI distribution, which could be calculated analytically (Appendix pp6-7). Since there is no natural reference BMI distribution to make comparisons against, we assessed the impact of eliminating low BMI on tuberculosis incidence by constructing counterfactual BMI distributions that

Specifically, we considered the effect of eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition (BMI<17kg/m2) or all undernutrition (BMI<18.5kg/m2). The left graph in Figure 1 illustrates the construction of a counterfactual BMI distribution (red) by eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition in this manner from a base case distribution (black). The relative risk of tuberculosis incidence for the counterfactual compared to base case distributions could again be calculated analytically (Appendix p7). Uncertainty in the slopes for the bilinear risk function was represented as a bivariate normal distribution based on variance-covariance matrix from the regression of Saunders et al.15

## Tuberculosis incidence and metrics calculated

To calculate the impact on tuberculosis incidence, we merged our estimates of relative reductions in each country, sex, and age group, with WHO estimates of tuberculosis incidence by country, sex, and age in 2023. Age groups used by WHO in their estimates are more aggregated than ours, and by default we assumed tuberculosis incidence was uniformly distributed over age sub-groups. Some countries provide tuberculosis notifications for the age 15-24 year groups separately. In these countries, sex-specific notification ratios were used to disaggregate 15-24 year incidence into 15-19 and 20-24 year age groups. For the WHO 65+ year age group, we used United Nations demographic estimates to split tuberculosis incidence proportional to population across 65-69, 70-74, 75-79, 80-84, and 85+ year age groups. For all estimates of tuberculosis incidence averted, we propagated uncertainty in incidence estimates analytically and combined it with uncertainty in relative risks and BMI distributions from 1,000 samples using the law of total variance. We computed the total tuberculosis incidence - and also proportion of tuberculosis incidence in each group - averted by eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition or all undernutrition, globally and by WHO region, for each sex and both sexes combined.  We computed the proportion of tuberculosis incidence averted in each age group by eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition or all undernutrition, globally and by WHO region, for each sex. Finally, we also calculated the proportion of tuberculosis incidence averted overall in each country by eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition or all undernutrition.

## Results

## BMI distributions

We obtained BMI distributions for 15 age groups, each sex, and 199 countries, representing >99% of the world population aged 15 years or older and >99% of estimated global tuberculosis incidence in this group. Of the 7600 country-sex-age groups that we fitted BMI distributions to, 7 failed to converge and were dealt with as described above. We estimated that, among those aged 15 years or older globally, 292 million (95% uncertainty interval[UI], 285 million to 300 million) had moderate/severe undernutrition and 615 million (95%UI, 607 million to 624 million) had undernutrition, representing 4.8% (95%UI, 4.7% to 5.0%) and 10.2% (95%UI, 10.1% to 10.3%) of this group respectively (Appendix Tables A2-3). The median for the prevalence of moderate/severe undernutrition across countries was 2.3% (interquartile range, 1.3% to 5.4%), and was 5.3% (interquartile range, 3.4% to 11.9%) for the prevalence of all undernutrition. The age distribution of the prevalence of both measures of undernutrition were U-shaped across all regions and both sexes (Appendix Figure A5). Prevalence of undernutrition globally was similar between sexes (a male:female ratio of 0.99 (95%UI, 0.94 to 0.99) for moderate/severe undernutrition), but varied by WHO region. The male:female ratio for moderate/severe undernutrition was close to one in South-East Asia (0.99 (0.91 to 1)), higher than one (i.e., more undernutrition in men than women) in the African [1.42 (95%UI, 1.23 to 1.35)] and Eastern-Mediterranean [1.23 (95%UI, 1.08 to 1.1)] regions, and below one elsewhere: 0.45 (95%UI, 0.42 to 0.51) in Europe, 0.8 (95%UI, 0.74 to 0.84) in the Americas, and 0.61 (95%UI, 0.57 to 0.64) in the Western Pacific regions.

## Global and regional incident tuberculosis averted

We estimated that eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition would avert 1.4 million (95%UI, 1.1 million to 1.7 million) tuberculosis episodes globally, and that eliminating all undernutrition would avert 2.3 million (95%UI, 1.8 million to 2.7 million) tuberculosis episodes globally (Table 1). This represents a 16.8% (95%UI, 14.3% to 19.2%) reduction in adult global tuberculosis incidence for eliminating moderate/severe undernutrition and a 26.5% (95%UI, 23.2% to 29.8%) reduction in global tuberculosis incidence for eliminating all undernutrition (Figure 2). The biggest decrease in tuberculosis incidence by eliminating all undernutrition would be seen for the South-East Asian region at 1.1 million (95%UI, 0.9 million to 1.4 million), followed by the African and Western Pacific regions (Table 1). Proportional reductions in tuberculosis incidence for eliminating all undernutrition would be largest in the South-East Asian [28.8% (95%UI, 25.2% to 32.3%)], African [28.4% (95%UI, 24.9% to 32.0%)], and Eastern Mediterranean regions [27.8% (95%UI, 22.1% to 33.4%); and lower in the Western Pacific [18.9% (95%UI, 14.8% to 23.0%)], the American [13.5% (95%UI, 11.1% to 15.9%)], and European [9.8% (95%UI, 7.9% to 11.8%)] regions.

## Tuberculosis averted by sex, age, and country

More tuberculosis episodes would be averted among men than women globally by eliminating all undernutrition (Table 1), in line with the larger number of global tuberculosis episodes among men. However, the proportion of tuberculosis incidence averted globally by eliminating all undernutrition would be slightly higher among women [28.8% (95%UI, 25.1% to 32.5%)] than men [25.2% (95%UI, 22.0% to 28.5%); Figure 2]. Moreover, these patterns vary by region. While the number of tuberculosis episodes averted would be higher in men than women for all regions except Europe, the proportion of tuberculosis incidence averted would be higher in women in all regions - up to twice as high in Europe (male:female ratio in proportion reduction 0.46 (95%UI, 0.32 to 0.59)). The highest number of tuberculosis episodes and proportions of tuberculosis incidence averted by eliminating all undernutrition would be seen in African and Asian countries (Figure 3). Eliminating all undernutrition would reduce tuberculosis incidence by over 25% in 47 countries: 30 countries on the African continent, six countries in South-East Asia, and six in the Americas (Appendix Figure A6). The proportion of tuberculosis incidence averted by eliminating all undernutrition globally showed a Ushaped dependence on age, with the highest proportions averted in adolescent and old-age populations (Figure 4). This pattern also varies by region, being larger in older age groups in the African region, and exhibiting asymmetric age patterns by sex in the African and European regions (Appendix Figure A7).

## Discussion

Our modelling suggests that nearly 2.3 million tuberculosis episodes in 2023 (27% of global tuberculosis incidence in adults) would be averted if all adults with undernutrition, representing 10% of this group globally, had their BMI increased above 18.5kg/m2. Strikingly, nearly 1.5 million tuberculosis episodes (17% of global tuberculosis incidence in adults) in 2023 would be averted if all adults with moderate/severe undernutrition, representing just 5% of this group globally, had their BMI increased above 17kg/m2. The proportion of tuberculosis incidence averted by eliminating undernutrition varied both between and within regions, and by sex and age, highlighting the importance of disaggregated data for informing policy decisions and allocation of resources. Broadly, our results suggest that the largest proportional reductions in incidence could be achieved by eliminating undernutrition in the African, South-East Asian, and Eastern Mediterranean regions; females; and adolescents and elderly adults. Our estimate that 27% of global tuberculosis incidence in adults could be averted by eliminating undernutrition, which is functionally equivalent to a PAF, is around three times higher than the most recent WHO PAF estimate of 8.9%.1 The WHO estimate uses a binary conceptualisation of nutritional status and risk, and a crude prevalence of undernutrition in each country to calculate the PAF, which is subject to methodological limitations. In contrast, we conducted a more refined analysis that used updated estimates for how tuberculosis risk changes non-linearly across the entire BMI range, and accounts for both the continuous nature of BMI as an exposure, and how BMI distributions differ across populations. Our estimates are similar to those of a previous study which generated revised PAF for undernutrition for 30 high tuberculosis burden countries.17 However, that analysis considered a limited number of countries and ages, and used an older risk estimate as input. While other modelling studies have also demonstrated the potential impact of changes in nutritional status on tuberculosis incidence to various degrees,18–24 none have provided comprehensive global estimates disaggregated by region, sex, and age. While we focussed on adults because of the different anthropometric indicators used in children, and lack of evidence on how nutritional status in children influences tuberculosis risk, our study highlights the need for further research in this population, given the overall importance of nutrition as a determinant of child development and mortality.25 These results highlight the fundamental importance of undernutrition in driving the global tuberculosis epidemic. While nutritional interventions for tuberculosis-affected households have been shown to be effective,9,26 their impact on the overall epidemic is likely to be limited because most Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission occurs outside of these households.10,27 Our results demonstrate the urgent need for further research exploring the health and economic impacts of population-level nutritional interventions extending beyond tuberculosis-affected households, including how these interventions should be designed and prioritised to most effectively prevent tuberculosis. This is more salient than ever given converging global crises that threaten to worsen both undernutrition and tuberculosis simultaneously. Global food insecurity has increased substantially since 2015, particularly in areas of the world with a high tuberculosis burden, driven by the COVID-19 pandemic and increasing global conflict.11,28 Climate change is projected to further challenge food security, both in the short-term due to extreme weather events and disasters, and in the longer-term because of effects on agriculture and

aquaculture productivity.29 Meanwhile, projected reductions in international donor funding through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria are expected to be catastrophic for tuberculosis, and global health more generally.30,31 Against this backdrop, nutritional interventions are already being deprioritised in favour of maintaining biomedical interventions,32 despite the fact they are likely to have myriad benefits extending beyond tuberculosis, including lowering child mortality,25 improving mental health,33  and enhancing economic productivity.34 Translating these findings into effective, sustainable public health interventions requires consideration of multiple factors. Nutrition-specific interventions, including direct food assistance and correction of micronutrient deficiencies, are essential for people with moderate/severe undernutrition, where our data suggest the greatest relative impact on tuberculosis incidence could be achieved. These are often delivered through maternal and child health interventions, or school-based programmes, and can be combined with nutritional counselling aiming to promote healthy nutritional behaviours. However, sustainable reductions in undernutrition (and preventing undernutrition from occurring) will require the expansion of these programmes to encompass undernutrition among adults, and incorporation of nutrition-sensitive approaches that address underlying structural and social determinants. These may include broader social protection interventions such as cash transfers, universal health coverage initiatives, and other social policies including subsidising healthy foods. At a population-level, these nutritional interventions could be targeted towards communities and households with high social vulnerability indices. Recent evidence from Brazil found lower tuberculosis incidence and mortality among beneficiaries of a targeted cash transfer programme with conditions around nutrition surveillance.35 Importantly, people at risk of tuberculosis often have multiple nutritional deficiencies, with both macro- and micro-nutrient deficiencies increasing risk.7 Vertical programmes targeting a small subset of these have been unsuccessful in reducing tuberculosis incidence.36 Therefore, interventions aiming to improve overall food security and nutritional status are likely to offer the greatest promise for reducing tuberculosis incidence. The broad scope of potential interventions raises important questions about funding responsibility, highlighting the need for more work to understand the budgetary and cost implications of scale-up. While tuberculosis-specific donors like The Global Fund have traditionally focused on biomedical interventions, addressing undernutrition at a population level requires coordination between health, development, and humanitarian funding streams, alongside stronger domestic financing and political commitment, including through innovative fund-raising mechanisms, e.g. taxes on sugary drinks or calorie-dense foods with little nutritional value. Furthermore, interventions must be designed with awareness of the double burden of malnutrition, as many settings now face coexisting undernutrition and obesity within the same communities.16 While the recent meta-analysis demonstrates that tuberculosis risk continues to decline across the entire BMI range, including in people with diabetes, and albeit at a slower pace among those who are overweight and obese,15 public health approaches must balance tuberculosis prevention goals with broader nutritional health objectives to ensure interventions do not inadvertently contribute to the growing burden of diet-related non-communicable diseases.37  Modelling the impact of population-level nutritional interventions beyond tuberculosis incidence to include mortality and morbidity from other diseases would help to inform this. Ultimately, further research is required to determine optimal nutritional interventions for different populations and settings. This should include participatory research
