methods with a broad range of stakeholders (e.g. civil society, government departments beyond health, and food system actors) to ensure interventions are locally appropriate, person-centred, and sustainable within existing systems.38 Our study has limitations. We applied a single risk function across all populations, though the doseresponse relationship between BMI and tuberculosis risk may vary by age, sex, and setting, given varying prevalence of HIV and other potential effect modifiers. Indeed, we may potentially be underestimating the impact of eliminating undernutrition by not accounting for potential synergistic interactions between nutritional status and other leading risk factors, such as alcohol use disorders which predispose to specific nutritional deficiencies.39 Our analysis also relied exclusively on BMI as an indicator of nutritional status, yet other dimensions of nutrition, including micronutrient deficiencies, and dietary diversity, quality, and composition, may influence tuberculosis risk independent of BMI.7 Importantly, our scenarios represent idealised interventions that eliminate all BMI values below arbitrarily defined thresholds. While these scenarios are unrealistic, as with PAFs, they serve to quantify the maximum theoretical impact of potential changes in nutritional status. Finally, we did not consider the impact of eliminating undernutrition on reducing tuberculosis mortality. Given undernutrition also increases the risk of adverse outcomes among people diagnosed and treated for tuberculosis, the proportion of tuberculosis mortality averted by eliminating undernutrition may be even larger than our estimates for incidence. In conclusion, our study demonstrates that eliminating undernutrition could prevent millions of individuals from developing tuberculosis - over a quarter of the current global adult tuberculosis incidence. The global tuberculosis response must urgently expand beyond biomedical interventions to address modifiable risk factors, which offer a critical pathway to achieving global targets that appear increasingly out of reach with current strategies. The scale-up of nutritional interventions, particularly for populations in greatest need, could have a substantial impact on the global tuberculosis epidemic while addressing a fundamental human right and delivering broader health, social, and economic benefits.

# Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study: a protocol for a quasi-experimental study to assess the impact of nutritional support on tuberculosis treatment outcomes in Benin and Togo

**Authors:** Chelsie Cintron; Madolyn Dauphinais; Attannon Arnauld Fiogbe; Mohammed Fall Dogo; Safiou Ate; Christine Adjonou; Kokou Agossou; Susie Jiaxing Pan; Marius Esse; Benjamin Ade; Komi Séraphin Adjoh; Dissou Affolabi; Pranay Sinha; Kobto G Koura

**Affiliations:** 1Medicine - Infectious Diseases, Boston Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease, Paris, Île-de-France, France | 3Programme National contre la Tuberculose, Cotonou, Benin | 4Unité de Suivi-Évaluation and Recherche, Programme National de Lutte Contre la Tuberculose, Lomé, Togo | 5Service de pneumologie, Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sylvanus Olympio, Lome, Golfe, Togo | 6Section of Infectious Diseases, Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 7Sciences Pharmaceutiques et Biologiques, COMUE Sorbonne Paris Cité, Paris, France

## Abstract

Undernourished persons with tuberculosis (TB) (PWTB) are at increased risk of mortality, treatment failure and relapse. Nutritional support for PWTB has the potential to mitigate the risk of undernutrition. However, given ethical concerns, well-powered randomised control trials of macronutrient support are unavailable to inform policymakers, clinicians and researchers about the impact of nutritional support. However, there is potential to understand the impact of macronutrient nutritional support through a natural experiment. Benin and Togo are neighbouring countries in West Africa. Benin’s national TB programme currently provides all PWTB with nutritional support whereas Togo’s national TB programme does not provide nutritional support to PWTB with drug-susceptible strains. Comparing treatment outcomes of PWTB treated in Benin and Togo can help us understand the impact of nutritional support for PWTB.

We designed a programmatic, prospective cohort study to assess the treatment outcomes among persons with pulmonary tuberculosis under programmatic conditions. PWTB cared for in Benin served as the exposed populations and those in Togo served as control. We plan to enrol 1050 adult participants across two countries: 700 subjects from Benin and 350 from Togo. We did not alter nutritional services offered to PWTB for the purposes of this study. Participants will be identified by the National Tuberculosis Programs of each country through 13 basic management units and followed until 6 months after treatment completion. The outcome of interest is a composite of all-cause mortality, treatment failure and relapse. Additional secondary outcomes will assess the effects on the rate of sputum conversion, loss to follow-up, weight gain, quality of life and post-TB lung health using surveys and a 6 min walk test. We hypothesise that participants receiving nutritional support will experience fewer unfavourable outcomes, faster sputum clearance, improved weight gain and fewer persistent respiratory symptoms.

This study has received approval from the Boston University Medical Campus and Boston Medical Center Institutional Review Board (H-43096). The study also received a favourable decision from the Benin Comité d’Ethique de la Recherche and approval from the Comité de Bioéthique pour la Recherche en Santé of Togo. Informed consent will be obtained from all study participants prior to their engagement in the research. Findings from the study will be disseminated via national and international conferences and through manuscript publications in peer-reviewed journals. Data can be made available upon request to the corresponding author.

NCT06084715. Pre-results.

- The Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study is the first of its kind to capitalise on existing programmatic differences between two countries to assess the impact of nutritional support on tuberculosis (TB) outcomes.

- The INSTITUT study will provide an opportunity to conduct a quasi-experimental analysis of nutritional support for persons with TB (PWTB), which is challenging to do through traditional randomised studies because of the lack of adequate equipoise.

- To our knowledge, the INSTITUT study is the largest programmatic assessment of nutritional interventions for TB in West Africa to date.

- Differences in the quality of TB management approaches in Benin and Togo may confound our analysis.

- Food sharing and food consumption outside of that provided by Benin’s national TB programme are not accounted for.

## Background

Undernutrition is the primary risk factor for tuberculosis (TB) globally, with an estimated population attributable fraction of 19%, surpassing 7.6% for HIV and 3.1% for diabetes.1 2 Although nutritional rehabilitation may reverse the immunological deficits associated with undernutrition, efforts to address undernutrition as a risk factor fall behind those of HIV and diabetes among persons living with TB (PWTB) and other at-risk populations.3 COVID-19, natural disasters and global conflicts have exacerbated food insecurity worldwide, disproportionately affecting high TB burden countries.4 The United Nations reported that COVID-19 led to a sharp increase in undernutrition with an estimated 118 million more people experiencing hunger in 2020 than in 2019.5 Climate change further threatens nutritional stability as droughts, floods, hurricanes, wildfires and other natural disasters disrupt both agriculture and food distribution systems.6 Interruptions to food production threaten the food security of vulnerable populations in areas with forced migration from ongoing conflict.7

Undernutrition, including both macronutrient and micronutrient deficiencies, resulting from poor dietary intake is widely prevalent and often life-threatening among PWTB.8 Poor nutritional status is associated with increased TB disease severity, as evidenced by higher bacillary burdens in the sputum, greater lung involvement and greater risk of cavitation.911 Undernourished individuals may also experience decreased drug absorption or increased drug toxicity.12 A large study in India found that each unit increase in baseline body mass index (BMI) was correlated with a 22% (95% CI 10% to 32%) reduction in mortality.13 Moreover, the inability to gain weight during the intensive phase of therapy is a marker for treatment failure, relapse and mortality.1416 These data underscore the significance of nutritional status on TB outcomes, and although the relationship between undernutrition and TB is bidirectional, the association between undernutrition and poor outcomes remains robust even after adjusting for confounders.

A systematic review of macronutrient supplementation for PWTB found evidence supporting nutritional interventions in promoting weight gain and accelerating sputum clearance.17 However, the results from this review are limited by the small sample size and heterogeneity. Some likely provided insufficient nutrients to detect an impact on critical TB-specific outcomes, such as mortality. Nonetheless, due to historical and contemporary data, there is insufficient equipoise to justify randomised controlled studies of providing nutritional support to persons with TB.3 4 The Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study hopes to address this lacuna by taking advantage of a natural experiment unfolding in Benin and Togo.

The Benin national TB programme currently offers programmatic nutritional support to all PWTB. In contrast, Togo’s national TB programme lacks a nutritional support component. The INSTITUT study aims to prospectively compare treatment outcomes across countries to understand the impact of programmatic in-kind nutritional support on nutritional recovery, treatment outcomes and post-TB lung health in West Africa.

## Methods

### Aims, objectives and outcomes

The INSTITUT project has two primary aims and outcomes: (1) to estimate the impact of nutritional support on TB treatment failure, death or relapse and (2) to estimate the impact of nutritional support on the nutritional status of PWTB at the end of treatment. The secondary aims of INSTITUT are to assess the effects of nutritional supplementation on the rate of sputum smear conversion at 2 months, weight gain during treatment (5% weight gain at 2 months; BMI at the end of treatment), quality of life and post-TB lung health as captured by persistent pulmonary symptoms and a 6-minute walk test. We hypothesise that participants receiving nutritional support will experience fewer unfavourable outcomes, faster sputum clearance, improved weight gain and fewer persistent respiratory symptoms.

### Study design and setting

The INSTITUT study is a programmatic, prospective cohort analysis conducted in national tuberculosis programme (NTP) hospitals in Benin and Togo in partnership with the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease and Boston Medical Center. The Republic of Benin has six data collection sites: (1) Basic Management Unit (BMU) Lazaret (National Teaching Hospital for TB and Respiratory Diseases (CNHU-PPC)), (2) BMU Calavi, (3) BMU Sèmè-Podji, (4) Godomey, (5) Akron and (6) Bethesda. The Togolese Republic has seven data collection sites: (7) Centre Hospitalier Universitaire Sylvanus Olympio (CHU SO), (8) BMU Adidogomé, (9) BMU Agoe Nyive, (10) Polyclinique Demakpoe, (11) Cs N’kafu, (12) Hopital de Be and (13) Centre de Sante Adakpame. 12 field teams of charge nurses, healthcare workers and a research assistant (Benin only) are responsible for study enrolment and participant follow-up. Enrolment began in September and November 2023 in Togo and Benin, respectively.

### Study population

Benin and Togo are neighbouring West African countries which are well suited for this study due to their demographic, socioeconomic and cultural similarities, which support meaningful comparisons. According to the World Bank, both countries have comparable population sizes, life expectancies and population growth rates.18 The GINI index—a measure of income inequality—is similar, with Benin at 34.4 and Togo at 37.9. Both countries also have similar TB incidence rates (Benin at 52/100 000 and Togo at 32/100 000) and receive financial and technical support from the WHO and the Global Fund for TB programmes.2 Additionally, both nations share overlapping ethnic and tribal groups, with individuals from the same cultural regions residing across borders, contributing to comparable dietary practices. These similarities ensure that participants from both countries can be meaningfully compared, though any residual differences will be addressed through appropriate statistical adjustments in our analysis. Moreover, both countries have similarly structured national TB programmes that have identical treatment protocols and frequently collaborate with each other.

We are enrolling persons with bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB who receive care at BMUs of NTP hospitals in Benin and Togo. Inclusion criteria are as follows: (1) age 18 years or older; (2) drug susceptible, GeneXpert MTB-RIF (Xpert) positive, and/or sputum smear positive (≥1+ acid-fast bacilli (AFB)); and (3) willing to attend follow-up visits and undergo study procedures. Exclusion criteria are as follows: (1) drug-resistant TB; (2) having received 7 or more days of antimicrobial therapy; (3) being too sick to enrol as defined as a score of 4 on the WHO Performance Status per study staff observation; (4) being pregnant at the time of enrolment; and (5) being unable to complete 6-min walk test due to pre-existing mobility issues due to disability, trauma, neurological compromise or cardiopulmonary disease. Enrolment is open to individuals with extrapulmonary TB; however, they must have evidence of pulmonary involvement to be eligible. To calculate power, we assumed that 10% of individuals not receiving nutritional support die or show evidence of treatment failure prior to end of therapy and approximately 5% of individuals would experience those outcomes. Further, we planned a 1:2 ratio between unexposed and exposed arms. To attain a power of 80% to detect this difference, we would need 334 unexposed participants and 676 exposed participants. In anticipation of 10% of participants withdrawing from the study, we increased our recruitment goals to 350 unexposed in Togo and 700 exposed participants in Benin. We expect to enrol 1050 subjects in total (figure 1).

*Figure 1: The Impact of Nutritional Support for Tuberculosis on Intermediate and Terminal Undernutrition and Treatment Outcomes (INSTITUT) study schematic.*

### Patient and public involvement

This is a programmatic study being conducted internally within the Programme National contre la Tuberculose (PNT) in Benin and the Programme National de Lutte contre la Tuberculose (PNLT) in Togo. As such, we did not partake in community engagement efforts. Ethical approvals were put in place to ensure that our research was consistent with the values of the participating countries. However, we plan to disseminate our findings to key community partners as well as the general public in addition to publishing our findings in academic journals.

### Study procedures, assessments and schedule

#### Consent and eligibility screening

PWTB are approached for study enrolment and consented in private at the BMU during their initial visit for TB care. Participants engage in extensive discussions of study objectives, procedures, and the risks and benefits of study participation with study staff before consenting to participate. Written informed consent is obtained from all participants prior to the performance of any study procedures. Staff conduct laboratory evaluation of sputum for nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) by Cepheid’s GeneXpert19 and AFB culture, chest radiograph (CXR), and a urine pregnancy test to determine eligibility status in women of childbearing age. NAAT results are obtained from medical records, and if unavailable at the time of enrolment, NAAT testing is performed. Sputum microscopy is performed on all participants, though subject to the participant’s ability to produce sputum. Chest radiography is completed at baseline if an X-ray has not been conducted previously. Women receive a urine pregnancy test prior to the CXR to prevent potential fetal radiation exposure. Medical history, socioeconomic status, and height and weight for BMI are collected in addition to the 6 min walk assessment. Height is measured using stadiometers and weight is measured using digital scales. Measurement has been standardised across all study sites with uniform equipment and calibration. The study team reviews all assessments and evaluation instruments in conjunction to determine participant eligibility using the study criteria.

#### Demographics, medical history and physical assessments

Demographic information is collected at baseline and during follow-up visits (months 2, 6 and 12). We collect information regarding socioeconomic status (global multidimensional poverty index)20 at baseline, alcohol consumption (Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Concise (AUDIT-C))21 at baseline, and quality of life (EuroQol 5 Dimension (EQ-5D))22 at baseline and follow-up visits (months 2, 6 and 12), as these factors may link to TB infection. Participants also complete a chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder (COPD) assessment23 at baseline and during follow-up visits (months 6 and 12).

#### Follow-up visits

Participants complete three follow-up visits after baseline: months 2, 6 and 12. Month 6 visit is conducted at the time of TB treatment completion, while month 12 visit is conducted 6 months post-treatment completion. During the month 2 visit, study staff conduct a sputum smear for those who can produce sputum. Study staff assess quality of life (EQ-5D) and medication adherence via pill counts and inspection of TB medication blister packs. Participants’ height and weight are reassessed for BMI determination. Through the national TB programme (NTP), Benin sites provide participants with nutritional supplementation.

During the month 6 and month 12 visits, study staff assess medical history, quality of life (EQ-5D), medication adherence via pill counts, and inspection of TB medication blister packs (month 6 only). Staff also administer a COPD assessment. We conduct a physical assessment of height and weight measurements for BMI determination as well as a 6 min walk assessment. Additionally, at the month 12 visit, participants receive a post-treatment CXR and we determine their final treatment outcome. Table 1 depicts study visit procedures.

### Benin nutritional supplementation

Benin’s NTP provides country-wide nutritional support to all PWTB. All persons with drug-susceptible TB are eligible for nutritional support through Benin’s national TB programme. The national nutrition programme is funded jointly by The Global Fund and the Government of Benin, though the government of Benin assumes two-thirds of the cost. The supplement, outlined in table 2, includes but not limited to components such as spaghetti, corned beef, powdered cassava (garri), condensed milk with sugar, sardines, sugar cubes, red beans, white beans, tomato paste, onions and sorghum (cereal grain). As there is no fixed food ration, the provided food basket comprises a rotation of the aforementioned food items for outpatient participants. The food type and quantity provided to PWTB are subject to the availability of ingredients and the BMU location. The frequency of food receipt is also variable dependent on availability. At most, PWTB will receive biweekly baskets and at minimum, once monthly. Hospitalised PWTH at Akron and Lazaret BMUs receive prepared meals three times per day.

### Data management

#### Data collection

All data are coded using participant identification numbers to maintain confidentiality. A designated study team member manually reviews the paper case report forms for completion and quality. A designated data coordinator is responsible for entering hardcopy data from paper forms into the online database, EpiData V.3.1.

#### Quality control

The investigational site is responsible for conducting routine quality assurance and quality control activities to internally monitor study progress and protocol compliance. The principal investigator and/or designated staff monitor these activities. Data checks are built into EpiData while a designated staff member also verifies digital data by reviewing electronic data against paper copies. We use this process to confirm the validity of the provided responses. We return any identified inconsistencies or incomplete forms to the field team for rectification. In addition, the Boston team performs routine data analysis and audits to evaluate the completion and consistency of data. Regular query reports are sent to the local teams and the team periodically visits the study sites to oversee data collection and entry.

#### Statistical analyses

The primary exposure is receipt of nutritional support which is limited to the Benin sites. The primary outcome will be a composite variable of unfavourable outcomes, including TB treatment failure, death or relapse based on evaluation 12 months after treatment initiation. An additional primary outcome will be BMI at the end of treatment and 1 year after treatment initiation. Secondary outcomes will be (1) sputum smear conversion at 2 months, (2) loss to follow-up during therapy, (3) quality of life as measured by EQ-5D score and (4) severity of post-TB chronic lung disease as captured by the validated COPD assessment test, degree of scarring on post-treatment chest radiograph, and 6 min walk test.

We will consider a comprehensive list of confounders including demographic factors (age, sex, urban vs rural residence), socioeconomic factors (multidimensional poverty index), disease-related risk factors (sputum smear grade, cavitation, cough duration, adherence, use of directly observed treatment, duration of hospitalisation, treatment support with community health workers), and comorbidities (BMI at start of treatment, HIV status and CD4 level, diabetes history, alcohol use, and tobacco use).

We will generate descriptive statistics for the primary dependent and independent variables as well as covariates. We will then pursue univariate analysis. χ2 analysis will be used for categorical variables and logistic regression will be used for continuous variables (age and years of education). We will calculate the variance inflation factor and set the cut-off at 5. We will remove redundant variables and possibly aggregate variables if appropriate. Finally, we will proceed with multivariable analysis with logistic regression. Age, sex and cough duration will be included in the multivariable analysis a priori. All covariates which are significant at p=0.2 will be included as well. We also plan a subgroup analysis of individuals in Benin who receive food only during the intensive phase and those who receive food through the entirety of their treatment. Additionally, we will apply causal inference techniques to address selection bias and strengthen the validity of our findings. Specifically, we will use propensity score matching to create balanced comparison groups between participants from Benin and Togo based on key baseline characteristics.

### Study expectations

In this study, we hypothesise that the risk of treatment failure or mortality is 50% lower among PWTB receiving nutritional support. Further, we hypothesise that the risk of remaining undernourished after TB treatment (defined as BMI <18.5 kg/m2) is 50% lower among those receiving nutritional support. We expect to quantify the impact of nutritional support on TB treatment outcomes. We anticipate that participants receiving nutritional supplementation as part of their TB care will have more favourable treatment outcomes compared with those who do not receive nutritional supplementation, faster sputum conversion, improved quality of life and less post-TB lung disease. Data from this study will allow us to inform TB policies by potentially identifying high-risk patient groups and improving disease management strategies throughout treatment.

## Discussion

The INSTITUT study allows us to assess the impact of nutrition on TB across two national TB programmes and gather data to inform the integration of nutritional supplementation in TB care locally and globally. Studying the impact of nutritional support on treatment outcomes using randomised clinical trials is ethically fraught as there is insufficient equipoise, particularly in light of the recent Reducing Activation of Tuberculosis by Improvement of Nutrition Status study24 as well as previously conducted interventional studies. The INSTITUT study offers a quasi-experimental alternative to answer this critical question by capitalising on the current differences in the nutritional support offered in Benin and Togo which have comparable health systems and populations.

One strength of this study is the strong partnership with TB programmes in adjacent, comparable countries allowing for a natural programmatic comparison and to implement testable hypotheses in a large population. The well-established nutritional programme in Benin is key to our understanding of the impact nutritional supplementation has on TB outcomes when compared with Togo’s programme which currently does not provide nutritional support. Further, within Benin, select BMUs provide extensive nutritional counselling alongside the food basket programme. We are positioned to understand the interplay of nutritional programmes, alone and in combination with nutritional counselling on TB outcomes. Our analyses also allow us to understand the effect of nutritional support on the nutritional recovery and quality of life of PWTB and whether nutritional support has potential as a host-directed therapy for post-TB chronic lung disease.

The study does have some potential weaknesses. This is a programmatic study that disallowed us from collecting large amounts of socio-demographic data. We also were unable to facilitate spirometry to assess for post-TB chronic lung disease outcomes and had to rely on validated survey data. Nutritional support provided in Benin is also not uniform across participants as it is provided ad hoc by the programme. We did not alter the nutritional composition of the programme as this was a programmatic study. The study design and financial limitations of the nutritional programme may result in dietary inconsistencies that will need to be accounted for during data analysis. Although we will employ causal inference methods to strengthen the analysis, the non-randomised nature of the study limits the extent to which we can draw definitive causal conclusions.

We expect that the provision of food will affect participants through numerous mechanisms, such as improving their food security, enhancing their immune response to TB, limiting drug toxicity and improving their adherence to TB medications.4 25 However, as this is a programmatic study, we are limited in the amount of data we can collect. While we do have records about the receipt of food baskets and the number of months individuals received support, we are not able to collect data on the number of calories consumed. Further, we acknowledge that participants may not consume the supplied food as intended and that provided food baskets are not the sole source of nutrition. Collecting dietary data through tools such as 24-hour recalls and food frequency questionnaires is labour intensive and, therefore, not possible in our study context. In addition, dietary records typically require literacy, which is not guaranteed among all study participants. Our study is designed to show that a policy action in terms of providing in-kind nutritional support may improve both nutritional and treatment outcomes. Additional mixed-methods research is crucial to understand the mechanisms by which such policy action can have its desired effect.

Currently, there is a paucity of data on the impact of nutritional support on TB treatment outcomes, particularly TB mortality and funding for TB—undernutrition research has been historically underfunded.26 The majority of the available evidence comes from India, which is a distinct epidemiological population with a lower rate of HIV.25 27 To catalyse policy change in West Africa, it is critical to generate local data on the impact of nutritional support programmes on TB outcomes. Doing so in a programmatic setting is also crucial as this provides a real-world assessment of effectiveness as opposed to efficacy in controlled experimental settings. This is the rationale behind our study. Further, this project directly supports South-South cooperation that allows two countries with expertise in TB care and nutritional support for PWTB to drive the creation and sharing of best practices for TB care across West African countries. Demonstration of a positive impact of nutritional support would provide a powerful impetus for implementing in-kind nutritional support in other African TB programmes. Indeed, evidence generated through the INSTITUT can be rapidly disseminated through close-knit networks such as the West and Central African Regional Network for TB control and has the potential to influence integration of nutritional care in TB programmes across the African continent.

### Ethics and dissemination

This study has received approval from the Boston University Medical Campus and Boston Medical Center Institutional Review Board (H-43096). The study also received a favourable decision from the Benin Comité d’Ethique de la Recherche and approval from the Comité de Bioéthique pour la Recherche en Santé of Togo. Informed consent will be obtained from all study participants prior to their engagement in the research. Findings from the study will be disseminated via national and international conferences and through manuscript publications in peer-reviewed journals. Data can be made available upon request to the corresponding author.

## Data availability statement

Data are available upon reasonable request.

# Tuberculosis and undernutrition: improving estimates to reinforce the policy imperative

**Authors:** Matthew J Saunders; Pranay Sinha; J Peter Cegielski; Rebecca A Clark; James A Seddon; Leonardo Martinez; Madhavi Bhargava; Anurag Bhargava; Richard G White; Rein MGJ Houben; C Finn McQuaid

**Affiliations:** 1Institute for Infection and Immunity, City St. George’s, University of London, London, UK | 2Faculty of Public Health and Policy, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, London, UK | 3Boston Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 4Section of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America. | 5Department of Epidemiology, Rollins School of Public Health, Emory University, Atlanta, USA | 6TB Modelling Group, TB Centre, and Centre for Mathematical Modelling of Infectious Diseases, Department of Infectious Disease Epidemiology, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, London, UK | 7Department of Infectious Disease, Imperial College London, London, United Kingdom | 8Desmond Tutu TB Centre, Department of Paediatrics and Child Health, Stellenbosch University, Cape Town, South Africa | 9Boston University School of Public Health, Department of Epidemiology, Boston, Massachusetts, United States of America. | 10Department of Community Medicine, Yenepoya Medical College, Mangalore, Karnataka, India | 11Department of Medicine, Kasturba Medical College Mangalore, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, Karnataka, India | 12Department of Medicine, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada

Undernutrition is a key driver of the tuberculosis epidemic, increasing the risk of developing tuberculosis and of poor outcomes in those who do so.1 Every year, the World Health Organization (WHO) publishes estimates of the number of tuberculosis episodes attributable to undernutrition and other risk factors, based on population attributable fractions (PAF). These allow stakeholders to compare the relative role of different risk factors in the tuberculosis epidemic, shaping policy and setting research agendas.

In 2023, WHO estimated a PAF of tuberculosis attributable to undernutrition of 17%; but in 2024 this was revised to 8.9%.2,3 Why? Because the two parameters used to calculate the PAF (prevalence of undernutrition and relative risk [RR] of tuberculosis associated with undernutrition) changed. In 2023, undernourishment – an indirect, modelled estimate of the percentage of the population with insufficient per capita energy availability to maintain a normal active and healthy life – was used as the exposure.2 However, the RR estimate used was derived from a systematic review of six studies showing a log-linear, dose-response relationship between body mass index (BMI) and tuberculosis. The RR of 3.2 (95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 3.1–3.3) compared tuberculosis incidence at a BMI of 16.0kg/m2 versus 25.0kg/m2.2,4 In 2024, undernutrition (BMI<18.5kg/m2 in adults) was the exposure, and the RR estimate used was 2.0 (95% CI: 1.7–2.2).3 This was extracted from a meta-analysis of four studies from a 2024 Cochrane review, which aimed to provide a simple binary estimate of the risk of tuberculosis associated with undernutrition versus no undernutrition (BMI≧18.5kg/m2).5

This shift to anthropometric measures is welcome,6 and we recognise WHO’s need for standardised, comparable metrics across risk factors based on systematic reviews addressing bias and heterogeneity. However, the Cochrane review’s approach paradoxically introduced new limitations that suggest the RR estimate used is likely underestimated. First, because of the emphasis on undernutrition as a binary exposure, several studies were excluded, including large cohorts included in the previous review and newer cohorts from settings with a high tuberculosis burden.7 Second, studies done in populations that may have a different RR of tuberculosis associated with undernutrition were inappropriately pooled, including adults and children, people with and without HIV and/or diabetes, and those with rare health conditions (e.g. post-gastrectomy). Third, definitions of undernutrition and particularly comparator groups (i.e. no undernutrition) differed between included studies, leading to classification inconsistencies. Fourth, the review did not adequately consider the previously established dose-response relationship between BMI and tuberculosis, demonstrated again in many of its included studies.8

Small, let alone large, errors in RR are important because the impact on the PAF and number of attributable cases is substantial (Figure 1). Our recent study provides revised and improved estimates using dose-response meta-analysis.9 This shows that tuberculosis risk is highest at the lowest BMI values and decreases non-linearly as BMI increases, with the steepest reduction in risk occurring when moving through underweight and normal weight ranges, and more modest reductions occurring through overweight and obese ranges. From our study, the estimated mean BMIs for people with and without undernutrition globally (i.e. below and above a BMI of 18.5kg/m2) sit at 17.0kg/m2 and 25.6kg/m2, which then gives an RR of 5.0 (95%CI: 4.2–5.9) and a PAF of 28.2%. Comparing 17.0kg/m2 with 21.8kg/m2 (the midpoint of the normal weight BMI category), the RR would be 2.8 (95%CI: 2.5–3.1) and the PAF 15.0%. By addressing the limitations of the previous approach, we show that current RR estimates used by WHO will substantially underestimate the population-level importance of undernutrition for the tuberculosis epidemic.

Consequently, policy decisions and allocation of resources may be directed away from this crucial determinant, leading to missed opportunities and diminished funding for nutritional interventions that could prevent tuberculosis and save lives. To ensure more accurate estimates moving forward, WHO PAF calculations for undernutrition should account for the dose-response relationship between BMI and tuberculosis, as well as the underlying distribution of BMI in different populations.10 To better characterise the relationship between nutrition and tuberculosis, future research should prioritise prospective cohorts with repeated anthropometric measurements using robust methods for tuberculosis diagnosis, particularly in underrepresented groups (e.g. children) from low- and middle-income countries; harmonise data collection protocols across cohorts; and utilise advanced analytical approaches to better account for heterogeneity (e.g. individual participant data meta-analyses, Bayesian hierarchical models).

The importance of undernutrition in driving the tuberculosis epidemic is high and warrants correct estimation. By using improved RR estimates alongside appropriate anthropometric measures, we enhance our understanding of the relative importance of undernutrition and ensure this critical determinant of tuberculosis receives the attention it deserves.

# Analysis of the Cross-Study Replicability of Tuberculosis Gene Signatures Using 49 Curated Human Transcriptomic Datasets

**Authors:** Xutao Wang; Katie Harper; Pranay Sinha; W. Evan Johnson; Prasad Patil

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Biostatistics, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, USA | 2Division of Computational Biomedicine, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, USA | 3Section of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, USA | 4Division of Infectious Disease, Center for Data Science, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, New Jersey, USA

## Abstract

Tuberculosis (TB) is the leading cause of infectious disease mortality worldwide. Numerous host blood-based gene expression signatures have been proposed in the literature as alternative tools for diagnosing TB infection. However, the generalizability of these signatures to different patient contexts is not well-characterized. There is a pressing need for a well-curated database of TB gene expression studies for the systematic assessment of existing and newly developed TB gene signatures.

We built curatedTBData, a manually-curated database of 49 human TB transcriptomic studies. This data resource is freely available through GitHub and as an R Bioconductor package that allows users to validate new and existing biomarkers without the challenges of harmonizing heterogeneous studies. We demonstrate the use of this data resource with cross-study comparisons for 72 human host blood-based TB gene signatures. For the comparison of subjects with active TB from healthy controls, 19 gene signatures had weighted mean AUC of 0.90 or greater, with the highest result of 0.94. In active TB disease versus latent TB infection, 7 gene signatures had weighted mean AUC of 0.90 or greater, with a maximum of 0.93.

The curatedTBData data package offers a comprehensive resource of curated human blood-based gene expression and clinically annotated data. This resource will facilitate the development of new signatures that are generalizable across cohorts or more applicable to specific subsets of patients.

## Introduction

Approximately 1.8 billion people in the world are estimated to be carriers the causative pathogen for tuberculosis (TB), Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often denoted as latent TB infection (LTBI), and about 10 million people develop ‘active’ pulmonary TB (PTB) each year worldwide [1]. Given the substantial prevalence of TB infections, timely and accurate diagnostics are critical. Sputum culture has been widely used for TB diagnosis, but it usually takes 6–7 days for a positive diagnosis and up to 42 days for a confirmed negative diagnosis [2]. Furthermore, while traditional sputum polymerase chain reaction (PCR) has become more common and offers faster results, its broader implementation is limited by cost. More recently, the introduction of GeneXpert MTB/RIF (CBNAAT) technology has significantly enhanced TB diagnosis, offering improved sensitivity and rapid detection across both pulmonary and extrapulmonary specimens. However, diagnostic challenges persist for paucibacillary TB like acid-fast bacilli smear-negative pulmonary TB or pediatric TB, and among individuals with certain comorbid conditions. As such, researchers have attempted to address these last diagnostic needs using blood-based gene expression signatures. For example, these have been developed for distinguishing active TB from LTBI, other bacterial and viral infections, and from healthy controls with high accuracy (among other applications). However, studies used to develop these host signatures often represent different geographical regions, distinct age groups, and cohorts with varying comorbid conditions [2, 3, 4]. As a result of this study heterogeneity, a single TB signature may exhibit poor generalizability in diverse patient populations [5, 6]. Variation in statistical procedures and overfitting of training models used to develop these signatures may also contribute to reduced generalizability [2, 7, 8].

As more host TB transcriptomic datasets become publicly available, there is greater opportunity to identify more robust and generalizable gene signatures for TB outcomes in diverse cohorts [9]. However, differences in gene expression platforms, annotation, pre-processing, and batch effects across studies often prevents users from making efficient use of these resources [10]. As a result, there is no current database of TB gene expression studies that provides researchers harmonized datasets for gene signature development and validation.

Here, we introduce the curatedTBData, an R data package available through GitHub and Bioconductor that harmonize 49 TB gene expression datasets for integrative analysis. The data are stores as MultiassayExperiment objects [11], enabling efficient management of raw data, normalized versions, metadata, and analysis results. Our standardized preprocessing pipeline (Figure 1) ensures consistent data handling across all studies.

To demonstrate the package utility, we conducted a systematic evaluation of 72 blood-based TB gene signatures [12] across selected datasets, focusing on distinguishing PTB from healthy controls (Control) and LTBI. Additionally, we demonstrate the use of an ensemble learning strategy that improves predictive performance by combining multiple gene signatures.

### Importance of curatedTBData

The landscape of human transcriptomic TB studies is characterized by small sample sizes and high heterogeneity. curatedTBData addresses this challenge by aggregating and harmonizing diverse datasets, enabling systematic validation of TB gene signatures at scale. By integrating data from multiple studies, researchers can gain deeper insights into TB biomarkers, assess their consistency, and explore sources of variability across studies.

Additionally, curatedTBData serves as a valuable resource for blood-based host biomarker discovery and validation, offering tools to analyze gene expression patterns, evaluate existing biomarkers, and uncover novel diagnostic insights. Its structured framework allows researchers to explore TB transcriptomics efficiently, supporting the development of robust and reproducible biomarkers.

## Methods and Implementation

### Study selection

We selected our studies using a stepwise process. Initially, priority was given to datasets that were used as training or discovery sets for signatures that are present in the TBSignatureProfiler R package [12]. Of the 49 datasets, 34 of them match these criteria. In addition, there are 11 datasets comprising 679 subjects, which corresponds to validation sets TB biomarkers as documented in relevant literature [2, 8, 6]. Curation of these datasets is an active, ongoing process, especially for additional biomarker training datasets. After identifying the datasets, we employed the R package GEOquery [14] to download them from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO). Of note, there are two datasets [15, 16] from the list that do not have GEO accession numbers (Table S2). For these studies, we followed the instructions provided in the respective papers to retrieve the raw/processed data. Finally, we have curated 49 TB transcriptomic datasets in the curatedTBData resource span 17 gene measurement platforms and contain clinical information for 4161 samples (Table S1). In order to access these datasets in a uniform way and to enhance the replicability of results across studies, we reprocessed these 49 datasets with manually curated clinical metadata information as described in Figure 1. For each transcriptomic study, both curated and raw data were included in the final output, and its reprocessing pipeline (in the form of R script) and related functions were also provided in the package (and in the Methods below).

### Metadata curation

For each study, we computationally and/or manually extracted the experimental, clinical, and demographic metadata by leveraging functions from the GEOquery [14] package. The curated metadata information was stored in the form of DataFrame, with standardized column names representing the different features (TBStatus, Gender, Age etc.) across different studies, and row names corresponding to each sample’s official GEO name. Moreover, the information within each feature was also aligned across datasets, so that users could efficiently subset samples based on certain criteria for meta-analysis. Finally, a standardized key of 60 variables to clinical and demographic information was summarized for current version of the curatedTBData (Table S2).

### Uniform preprocessing RNA-sequencing data

We reprocessed each RNA sequencing dataset from the raw FASTQ files. The downloaded sequence data were first trimmed using Trimamomatic-0.36 [17] to remove low quality reads (SLIDINGWINDOW=4:20, LEADING=3, TRAILING=3, MINLEN=36). The trimmed data were then aligned to NCBI RefSeq gene annotations hg38 (for all RNA-seq studies) and hg19 (for selected RNA-seq studies where hg19 was used in their original paper); lastly, the mapped reads for genomics features were counted using the package Rsubread [18, 19]. The pipeline for reprocessing RNA-Seq datasets is available on the GitHub page for our paper. We validated the reprocessed results by plotting the correlation between the reprocessed RNA-Seq data and its corresponding original data from GEO.

### Data storage, functionality, and package access

In the package, the S4 object MultiAssayExperiment [11] was implemented to store all the information for each study. This data structure is beneficial for representing and analyzing multi-omics experiments. The curatedTBData package takes the advantage of using the MultiAssayExperiment to retain raw expression profiles, normalized expression profiles, and different versions of the data etc. In such case, users can efficiently manage and access both raw and multiple processed/harmonized version of each study. Additionally, object of MultiAssayExperiment from the curatedTBData can be converted to SummarizedExperiment object easily, enabling users to leverage toolkit from other packages (i.e. TBSignatureProfiler).

The curatedTBData provides analytic utility functions for biomarker validation along with comparative visualizations including, boxplot, heatmap, and ridgeplot. Additionally, the package includes the function subset_curatedTBData, which allows users to subset samples based on input conditions, and the function combine_object, which facilitates the combination of datasets with common gene names. It is important to note that while there are various methods for data integration, such as ComBat among other tools [20, 21, 22], the current version of this package does not offer any specific methods for integration. Users are encouraged to choose integration techniques based on their specific need and preferences.

The curatedTBData package utilizes the ExperimentHub [41] to host its resource, enabling quick access with efficient memory usage. Datasets are stored on the ExperimentHub web service, and once the package is installed, users can retrieve the entire dataset collection or selectively access specific studies of interest using the curatedTBData function (which shares the package name). This process does not require high-performance computing and can be performed locally in R or RStudio with on a standard laptop with 16GB RAM or less. The processing time for each dataset ranges from 30 seconds to 1 minute, depending on the study size. For detailed instructions on accessing the datasets, please refer to the following tutorial:

### Bioconductor curatedTBData Tutorial.

#### Datasets and gene signatures used for comparative analysis

For demonstration purpose, we compared the performance of 72 human host TB gene signatures for their content and metadata for differentiating patients with PTB from Control or from LTBI. These gene signatures were downloaded from the TBSignatureProfiler as of October 2023. In addition, the description of the gene lists for these 72 gene signatures can be found in the supplementary material. Study selection/combination and sample selection process was conducted before the comparative analysis (Figure 2). Specifically, datasets with only PTB subjects or that focus on progression analysis were excluded (n = 8), as well as subjects with HIV, diabetes, and involved in repeated measurement other than baseline were excluded. In conclusion, 19 studies comparing patients with PTB to those with LTBI, and 15 studies comparing patients with PTB to healthy controls, were included for subsequent comparative analysis.

Because the gene sets which define each model are often more readily available than the original signature model itself, we chose to perform the comparative analysis using two uniform single-sample methods: 1. Single-Sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA) [23] and 2. Pathway Level Analysis of Gene Expression (PLAGE) [24], which represent two competitive and self-contained gene set scoring methods [25]. ssGSEA calculates a sample-level gene set score by comparing the distribution of gene expression ranks inside and outside the gene set [23]; whereas PLAGE standardizes expression values and applies singular value decomposition (SVD) for the genes within the gene set. The activity level of a pathway in a given sample is taken as the coefficient of the first right-singular vector [26]. The R package GSVA [27] was implemented to compute scores from ssGSEA and PLAGE. There are chances that some of genes within gene sets were missing across multiple transcriptomic datasets, primarily due to different versions for the name of the gene symbols or the inconsistent gene coverage across sequencing platforms. To alleviate this problem, the R package HGNCHelper [28] was used to update gene symbols for both TB gene signatures and transcriptomic datasets.

#### Cross-study ensemble learning

Integrating information from different biomarkers is one of the critical applications of the curatedTBData database [13]. In the context of ensemble stacking strategy [29], we treated multiple gene signatures collectively as a single predictor, termed as the ‘meta-predictor‘. Subsequently, ensemble learning models were trained based on data from multiple studies to assess the performance of this composite predictor.

As a demonstration exercise, 34 host TB gene signatures has been selected in the example case of usage, and the list of signatures for training an ensemble model are shown in Figure S6. Additionally, datasets with sample size less than 15 were excluded from ensemble analysis. These datasets frequently exhibited strong signal among different TB subtypes, with a majority of biomarkers demonstrating high predictive accuracy for them. Finally, a total of 14 datasets for PTB vs. Control and 14 datasets for PTB vs. LTBI had been included in the example.

The procedures for performing ensemble analysis were listed as follows. Firstly, a subset of signatures with size S were randomly sampled without replacement to investigate how the ensemble process varies across different gene sets ( S = 5 in this example). Consider K training datasets and V validation datasets of dimension n k × g k , where k = 1 , 2 , … , K + V . Additionally, we have an outcome variable Y k ∈ R n k representing the disease status or control cases for individuals. The aim of ssGSEA or PLAGE is to transform each n k × g k gene expression profile into a n k × S gene set enrichment matrix. This transformation ensures that each dataset now shares the same set of predictors, namely the predicted scores derived from each gene signature. In this study, the objective of the ensemble approach is to predict outcomes in the validation datasets v using a linear combination of the predicted scores for each of gene set.

We define the predicted scores obtained from training data k and gene set s as Y ˆ k ( s ) . Subsequently, we stack the predicted score from the group of K datasets for gene set s to be Y ˆ ( s ) ∈ R N , where N = ∑ k n k . The true outcomes from the K datasets are represented as Y = Y k ∈ R N . Finally, the predicted results to a set of combined gene sets are denoted as Y ˆ = [ Y ˆ ( S ) ] N × S . We determine weights w = w 1 , … , w s that correspond to a set of combined gene signature scores based on the Lasso where m i n w ∈ R S + 1 | | L ( Y , Y ˆ , w ) | | 2 + λ | | w | | 2

The final predicted score for the meta-predictor on validation dataset v is given by Y ˆ v = ∑ s = 1 S w S Y ˆ ( s )

The performance of the ensemble sets on each validation study was evaluated using A U C , and its overall validation performance was determined by the weighted mean A U C values ( A U C w ) across V validation studies: AUC = ∑ v = 1 V AUC ( Y v , Y ˆ v ) V

The variation of the A U C s for both ensemble sets and gene signature across n studies, each with observations: w 1 , … , w n and A U C s : A U C 1 , … , A U C n , were evaluated using the weighted standard deviation ( S D w ) and showed in the form of ridge plot (Figure S8) where S D w = ∑ i = 1 n w i ∗ ( A U C i − A U C w ¯ ) n - 1 with w i ∗ = w i ∑ i = 1 n w i , A U C w ¯ = ∑ i = 1 n w i × A U C i ∑ i = 1 n w i

To reduce the bias of test study selection, we performed cross-study validation by repeatedly splitting the multi-studies into K training and V testing datasets for M iterations. For the group of datasets with size N ( N = 14 for both comparisons in this example), we randomly selected 80 % of studies as training data with K = ⌊ 0.8 N ⌋ and the remaining as testing data with V = N − K for M = 300 iterations.

### Statistics used for evaluation

For each TB gene signature, its performance in distinguishing different phenotype was be evaluated by the AUC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristics Curve), sensitivity, and specificity value, calculated by the R package pROC [30]. The sample-size weighted average AUC values (weighted AUCs), sensitivity values (weighted sensitivity), and specificity values (weighted specificity) were computed across datasets to evaluate the overall performance for each gene signature. The 95% confidence interval for these metrics was calculated over 1000 bootstrapped subsampling. Finally, the performance of ensemble of group signature was also compared with its single best subset using the weighted student’s t-test, implemented by the function wtd.t.test from R package weights [31].

## Results

### Overall Performance of TB Gene Signatures

For the comparison of PTB vs. Control, three gene signatures (Blankley_5, Kaul_3, and Tabone_RES_27) out of 72 achieved the highest weighted AUCs of 0.94 (95% CI: 0.87 - 0.98) when assessed using ssGSEA; Conversely, another set of three gene signatures (Maertzdorf_15, Suliman_4, and Tabone_OD_11) had the highest weighed AUCs of 0.94 (95% CI: 0.88 - 0.98) using PLAGE (Table S3). For the comparison of PTB vs. LTBI, Bloom RES_268, Estevez_133, and Tabone_RES_27 had the highest weighted AUCs of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.84 - 0.98) using ssGSEA; while Kaforou_27 yielded the highest weighted AUCs of (0.93, 95% CI: 0.87 - 0.97) using PLAGE (Table S3).

Overall, 67 gene signatures demonstrated weighted AUCs ≥ 0.80 in at least one comparison using either ssGSEA or PLAGE (Figure 3A). Notably, 43 (64.2%) gene signatures had weighted AUCs ≥ 0.80 in distinguishing patients with PTB from either Control or LTBI, irrespective of the evaluation methods (PLAGE or ssGSEA). Additionally, eight (11.9%) gene signatures with weighted AUCs ≥ 0.80 were found in both comparisons using PLAGE (Figure 3A). Moreover, 35 gene signatures had weighted AUCs ≥ 0.90 in at least one comparison using either ssGSEA or PLAGE, with four (11.4%) gene signatures (Blankley_5, Kaforou_27, Kaul_3, and Tabone_RES_27) consistently maintaining weighted AUCs ≥ 0.90 across all four comparisons (Figure 3B). In summary, a greater number of gene signatures showed high predictive ability (weighted AUCs ≥ 0.90) in PTB vs. Control (n = 33) compared to PTB vs. LTBI (n = 22; Figure 3B).

For PTB vs. Control, the highest weighted sensitivity was observed with Kaul_3 (0.92, 95% CI: 0.80 - 0.99) using ssGSEA, while Maertzdorf_15 and PennNich_RISK_6 achieved a weighted sensitivity value of 0.91 (95% CI: 0.75 - 0.99) using PLAGE (Table S4). Additionally, Blankley_5, Hoang_OD_20, and Roe_3 demonstrated the highest weighted specificity of 0.94 (95% CI: 0.81 - 1.00) using ssGSEA, and the highest weighted specificity was given by Natarajan 7 (0.94, 95% CI: 0.83 - 0.99) using PLAGE (Table S5).

For PTB vs. LTBI, Thompson 9 exhibited the highest weighted sensitivity (0.87, 95% CI: 0.71 - 0.97) when evaluated by ssGSEA, and Suliman 4 had the highest weighted sensitivity (0.88, 95% CI: 0.74 - 0.98) using PLAGE (Table S4). Moreover, the highest weighted specificity was given by Bloom_OD_144 and Tornheim_71, both recording a value of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.77 - 0.99) using ssGSEA, and Thompson_9 achieved the highest weighted specificity of 0.94 (95% CI: 0.81 - 1.00) using PLAGE (Table S5).

### Individual Performance of TB Gene Signatures

The evaluation of gene signature performance within individual datasets is presented in Figure S1 and Figure S2. In the context of PTB vs. Control, both ssGSEA and PLAGE encountered difficulties computing profiling scores for Kulkarni_HIV_2 (INSL3, RAB20 ) in three out of 25 datasets. Notably, either one of the genes were not found in GSE6112 and Bruno study [32], while both genes were not identified in GSE74092 (Figure S1). For PTB vs. Control, the predictive performance of seven gene signatures were unavailable in GSE6112, mainly because the use of the MPIIB custom human sequencing platform. Additionally, profiling scores for 13 gene signatures profiling score were not accessible in GSE74092, given its utilization of an RT-PCR assay (Figure S1). Regarding the comparison of PTB vs. LTBI, results for six gene signatures (Tabone_OD_11, Gong_OD_20, Kulkarni_HIV_2, Suliman_4, Roe_3, and Kaul_3) were unavailable in GSE6112 (Figure S2).

### Ensemble of multiple gene signatures

Ensembles of multiple gene signatures in differentiating subjects with PTB from Control or from LTBI were also implemented as an application and compared using the curatedTBData package. In this practice, 30 ensemble sets with each set contain 5 gene signatures had been evaluated for both comparisons, and as expected, the performance of ensemble gene signatures varied greatly set by set (Figure S5; Figure S8). Overall, for the comparison of PTB vs. Control, 25 out of 30 ensemble sets demonstrated higher weighted AUCs when compared to their single best gene signature, whether evaluated using PLAGE (n = 17) or ssGSEA (n = 18; Figure S5A). Specifically, 8 out of 17 sets had smaller weighted SD using PLAGE, and 17 out of 18 sets had smaller weighted SD using ssGSEA (Figure S8A). In the context of PTB vs. LTBI, all ensemble sets outperformed their single best subset, whether assessed through PLAGE (n = 6) or ssGSEA (n = 29; Figure S5B). Among these sets, 5 out 6 had lower value of weighted SD with PLAGE, and 14 out 16 had lower value of weighted SD with ssGSEA (Figure S8B). Three selected ensemble sets were highlighted to illustrate the distinct performance of ensembling biomarkers (Figure 4, 5).

### Active TB vs. Control

Ensemble Set 6 exhibited a weighted AUC of 0.90 (95% CI: 0.89 - 0.91) when evaluated by PLAGE, a value significantly smaller than its single best gene signature, Roe_3 (0.92, 95% CI: 0.91 - 0.93; p-value = 9.0e – 3). Additionally, Set 6 demonstrated a smaller value of weighted SD (SDw = 0.024) in comparison to Roe 3 (SDw = 0.021) and Anderson_42 (SDw = 0.021) using PLAGE. When assessed by ssGSEA, Set 6 had significantly higher weighted AUCs (0.93, 95% CI: 0.92 - 0.94) when compared to its best subset Roe_3 (0.91, 95% CI: 0.90 - 0.92; p-value < 1.0e – 3; Figure 4A), and had the smallest weighted SD (SDw = 0.016) when evaluated by ssGSEA (Figure 5A).

Although Set 21 displayed similar weighted AUCs to its highest subset, Laux-daCosta_OD_3 (0.92, 95% CI: 0.91 - 0.93; p-value = 0.78) according to PLAGE (Figure 4A), it had the smallest weighted SD (SDw = 0.024) when compared to all other gene signatures within the ensemble set (Figure 5A). When evaluated by ssGSEA, Set 21 significantly outperformed its single best gene signature, Tornheim_71 (0.91, 95% CI: 0.90 - 0.93; p-value < 1.0e–3; Figure 4A) and as anticipated had the lowest weighted SD among all the five gene sets (SDw = 0.016; Figure 5A).

For Set 22, its weighted AUCs were comparable to the results from Zak_RISK_16 using either PLAGE or ssGSEA (p-value > 0.05 for both methods; Figure 4A). However, Set 22 had the smallest weighted SD when compared to any of gene signature within the ensemble set for both methods (SDw = 0.016 for PLAGE and SDw = 0.015 for ssGSEA; Figure 5A).

### Active TB vs. LTBI

Ensemble Set 6, characterized by a weighted SD of 0.014 for PLAGE and 0.015 for ssGSEA, demonstrated superior performance compared to its single best gene signature, Roe_3 (SDw = 0.019) and Bloom_OD_144 (SDw = 0.016) using both PLGAE and ssGSEA (p-value < 0.01 for both methods; Figure 4B; Figure S8B). The performance of Set 21 (0.88, 95% CI: 0.87 - 0.88, SDw = 0.022) was significantly inferior to its best subset Anderson_OD_51 (0.91, 95% CI: 0.90 - 0.93, SDw = 0.019) using PLAGE (p-value < 1.0e – 3; Figure 5B). Conversely, when ssGSEA was the profiling method, Set 21 (0.92, 95% CI: 0.91 - 0.93) significantly outperformed its best subset, Tornheim_71 (p-value < 1.0e – 3, SDw = 0.019; Figure 4B), with the smallest weighted SD of 0.012 (Figure 5B). Lastly, Set 22 (SDw = 0.021) exhibited smaller weighted AUCs compared to its best subset, Berry 393 using PLAGE (p- value = 0.011, SDw = 0.019; Figure 4B, 5B). In contrast, Set 22 (SDw = 0.016) outperformed it best subset, Zak_RISK_16 (SDw = 0.020) using ssGSEA, with the smallest weighted SD among all of its subsets (p-value < 1.0e – 3; Figure 4B, 5B).

### TB Gene Signatures Performance across HIV or diabetes status

In extending the use of the curatedTBData resource, we evaluated the efficacy of the72 gene signatures in distinguishing active TB from control cases within HIV- positive and HIV-negative populations based on the results given by ssGSEA and PLAGE (Figure S3). The distribution of AUCs suggested that, for both methods, most of the gene signatures had lower predictive ability in identifying active TB from controls among study participants with HIV infection when compared to study participants with HIV infection (Figure S3). This suggests a significant impact of HIV status on existing TB biomarker performance. As another application, we showcased the distribution of nine signatures’ scores across healthy control cases, subjects with active TB, subjects with diabetes, and subjects with active TB and diabetes co-infection in Bruno et al. (Figure S4). When evaluating the data using PLAGE, gene signatures consistently showed higher enrichment scores in the healthy control group and those individuals with diabetes, compared to the other two conditions. Conversely, results based on ssGSEA revealed that these signatures consistently presented lower enrichment scores within the healthy controls and diabetic subjects (Figure S4). Although these two methods indicate a distinct gene signature response pattern across different patient statuses, they are both capable of distinguishing individuals with active TB from those without. However, all 9 signatures have poor performance in the comparison within healthy controls and diabetic individuals, as well as between active TB cases and those with TB and diabetes co-infection (Figure S4).

## Discussion

In this paper, we introduced the curatedTBData data package for R statistical programming environment. Currently, this package includes 49 TB transcriptomic datasets with well-annotated metadata, which serves as a curated resource that allows researchers to make efficient use of currently existing human TB gene expression profiles. One of the most important outstanding problems for public transcriptomic TB datasets is that some of studies lack clinical information, and others may possess inconsistent definition of clinical features across different datasets [33].

In our curation efforts, we were able to retrieve important clinical characteristics including age, gender, geographical region, TB status, etc., for most of the studies. However, features such as TB diagnostic methods remained inconsistent across many of the studies due to their original design. Currently, there are various techniques to diagnose TB outcomes including but not limited to sputum culture, sputum PCR, sputum microscopy, bronchoalveolar lavage (bal) culture, and biopsies. LTBI is assessed using tuberculin skin test (TST), and Interferon-Gamma Release Assays (IGRAs), which – if positive – reflect exposure, but are unable to speak to past infection that has resolved as opposed to ongoing latent infection. Most datasets used either one or combined technique(s) to identify a patient’s TB status, while there are some studies that do not contain TB diagnostic information (Table S2). The relatively large number of well-annotated studies in this database could contribute to future work that recover missing clinical annotations.

While there are several approaches that discussed the problems about dealing with multiplicative Affymetrix probesets or Ensembl IDs [34]; in the current version of the data package, we used the naive method by taking the median value of the probes/Ensembl IDs that target the same gene. For the output of the MultiassayExperiment object, the updated gene expression data with gene symbols as row names were showed in the slot with name assay_curated, and the un-collapsed version of the data were also provided in the slot with assay_raw. In summary, this heterogeneous database is a representation of clinical practice as patients were diagnosed using different methods, and it also represents heterogeneity in both host and pathogen genetics [2].

To demonstrate the utility of this resource, we analyzed gene signatures distinguishing PTB from LTBI and healthy controls. To obtain clear TB-specific signatures, we analyzed subjects without comorbidities like HIV or diabetes, as these conditions significantly alter immune responses and gene expression profiles. The exclusion also shows a strength of the curatedTBData resource, which lies in its scale and flexibility. The dataset is large enough to allows stratified analyses, enabling researchers to investigate TB biomarker both in the presence and absence of these comorbidities. Indeed, we conducted additional analyses of TB signatures in individuals with HIV and diabetes (Figure S3; Figure S4), showcasing how this resource can be used across diverse clinical contexts.

In our comparative analysis, gene signature scores across samples were computed using ssGSEA and PLAGE. While some studies [2, 7] have utilized the original models from which the signatures were derived, we advocate for the use of gene set scoring methods due to their uniformity, accessibility, and robustness. Previous research [12, 35] has also applied these methods for comparative purposes, reinforcing its reliability. Consistent with the literature, we believe that implementing ssGSEA and PLAGE allows for a fair and reproducible evaluation of TB gene signature performance.

These methods offer distinct approaches to summarizing gene set activity. ssGSEA ranks genes within a set relative to those outside of it, making it well-suited for large-scale RNA-seq data but potentially less applicable to PCR-based methods, where the number of measured genes is limited. Additionally, due to its ranking-based design, ssGSEA may produce null enrichment scores when a gene set contains both upregulated and downregulated genes, as their effects can cancel each other out [36]. In contrast, PLAGE, a PCA-based method, computes gene set scores relative to the study cohort using only the genes within the set. This makes PLAGE less sensitive to the specific distribution of up- and downregulated genes but more susceptible to variability introduced by heterogeneous study designs.

Our analysis revealed that larger number of TB gene signatures had high diagnostic ability (weighted AUCs ≥ 0.90) in the comparison of PTB vs. Control when compared to PTB vs. LTBI (Table S3; Figure 3). Meanwhile, the selection of profiling methods did not have significant impact on gene signatures’ predictive ability in PTB vs. Control (p-value = 0.12). However, in PTB vs. LTBI, PLAGE outperformed ssGSEA (p-value ≤ 1.0e – 3; Table S3; Figure 3). This outperformance may be attributed to the fact that gene signatures were pre-selected based on prior knowledge, and PLAGE, by applying dimension reduction techniques, effectively captures their underlying biological significance [26].

While we did not explore the choice of gene set scoring methods in exhaustive detail, our findings suggest that the original platform used to derive a gene signature (mRNA-seq vs. PCR) has a minimal impact on the choice of scoring method. Instead, factors such as the composition of the gene set and the study design play a more significant role.

Generally, ensemble learning of multiple TB gene signatures were able to improve the overall predictive ability. This outperformance was expected, as ensemble stacking technique combines information from each of single learner, yielding higher accuracy results [37]. Additionally, the performance of ensemble sets in PTB vs. LTBI exhibited superiority compared to the PTB vs. Control (Figure S5). It is noteworthy that the results were not directly comparable due to different samples were included in these two comparisons. From an ensemble stacking perspective, gene signatures in the context of PTB vs. LTBI may be considered as weak learners in contrast to PTB vs. Control (Figure 3), and the advantage of ensemble technique lies in enhancing model performance by combining weak learners [37, 38].

In our practice, large weights were assigned to those with high predictive ability on average (Table S3; Figure S6). For example, gene signatures like Zak_RISK_16, Kaforou_27, and Blankley_5 etc., had consistently non-zero weights whenever they were included in the ensemble sets(Figure S6). One large deficient were shown in Set 28 with PLAGE (Figure S5) for both comparisons. This was primarily because Set 28 mistakenly shrank the coefficient for signatures with high predictive ability to zero (i.e. Berry_393 in PTB vs. Control and Estevez_133 in PTB vs. LTBI) (Figure S5), which also suggested the instability of using PLAGE in the context of stacking ensemble.

Although the outperformance of ensemble sets was trivial in terms of weighted AUCs (outperformance up to 3%), the consistency of the results were increased by leveraging ensembling strategy (Figure S8). While individual biomarkers may perform well in discriminating between active TB and other groups, our results reveal a surprising finding: ensembling establishes a robust baseline for performance across multiple datasets. The ensembling approach offers insights in improving signature performance when we do not have prior knowledge of which signatures would perform better in the given data. Although in the comparison of PTB vs. Control using PLAGE, only 8 out of 17 sets had a lower value of weighted SD. However, in all other comparisons, a high percentage (more than 83%) of ensemble sets exhibited increased stability compared to their corresponding single best signature (Figure S8). The reduction of variation for model is another critical pattern of ensemble strategy. It has also been shown in some empirical studies that the improvement of model performance was attributed to the reduction of variance to some extents in voting algorithm including Bagging and Boosting [38, 39].

For both comparisons, the performance of ensemble sets given by ssGSEA was better than the performance given by PLAGE. The outperformance of ensemble of gene signatures using ssGSEA was possibly due to the results scores given by ssGSEA were rank-based and single-sample, which were robust against heterogeneous datasets and does not depend on other samples in the datasets [36]. Moreover, large variations of the profiling scores were given by ssGSEA (SDPTB = 0.17, SDLTBI = 0.154, SDControl = 0.15) when compared to PLAGE (SDPTB = 0.033, SDLTBI = 0.034, SDControl = 0.031; Figure S7), which is critical for the outperformance of ensemble learning [40]. In addition, the coefficient for selected gene signatures were more likely to be positive using ssGSEA when compared to the results from PLAGE (Figure S6), this is largely due the resulting scores given by ssGSEA for most of gene signatures in ensemble, on average, were higher for PTB when compared to Control or LTBI (except Anderson_42 and Verhagen_10 for PTB vs. Control, and Suliman RISK_4 and Thompson_FAIL_13 for both comparisons; Figure S7).

Our ensemble approach not only provides a new insight into existing biomarkers but also serves as a tool to develop more robust predictive signatures. By integrating multiple biomarkers, ensemble method provides a performance baseline, often matching or exceeding individual biomarkers. Rather than being a strict requirement for clinical implementation, ensembling is primarily a research tool designed to aid biomarker discovery and validation. A key example is the Sweeney 3-gene signature [42], which was developed through the integration of multiple datasets, requiring significant effort. Our work aims to streamline this process by creating resources that enable the systematic development and evaluation of similar biomarkers. This ensemble approach supports clinical and translational researchers in selecting transcript-level markers for validation in clinical assays by enhancing biomarker robustness, providing a performance baseline, and facilitating systematic biomarker development.

## Conclusion

### Contribution Summary

The curatedTBData package offers an extensive resource of curated gene expression and clinically annotated data for various applications, including but not limited to the comparative analysis of existing TB gene signatures and the discovery of new TB gene signatures. This database provides researchers to make efficient use of TB gene expression data and offers a resource for reproducible and replicable analysis of the TB transcriptomic datasets.

In the context of TB diagnostics using blood-based biomarkers, it is important to evaluate existing gene signatures in a systematic way. Our comparative analysis showed that 65 out of 72 gene signatures were able to separate patients with PTB from healthy controls or LTBI with high accuracy (weighted AUCs ≥ 0.8) using either one of the two gene set scoring methods, and gene signatures tend to have higher accuracy in distinguishing PTB from Control when comparing to PTB from LTBI (Figure 3). Our results provided strong evidence for the diagnosis of TB using blood-based biomarkers, as well as the evaluation of TB gene signatures using gene set scoring methods. We also showed that ensemble methods establish a performance baseline, ensuring that predictions are at least as reliable as individual signatures, if not better. This technique is recommended for biomarker discovery and validation, especially for selecting biomarkers in heterogeneous testing cohorts.

### Limitation and Next Steps

Our analysis has a few limitations. When building curatedTBData, the mapping of probe sets to common gene symbols is critical for promoting cross-study consistency. However, gene identification is a persistent problem in integration analysis [10]. We primarily used information from GEO as the reference, but that information may have updated with the development of sequencing technology. Also, when evaluating the performance of 72 gene signatures, we did not use the discovery model for each signature from its original study. For some gene signatures, certain underlying information may be lost if we used gene set enrichment analysis to evaluate their performance. Moreover, for some gene signatures, some genes were not available across different studies. Although we used the R package HGNCHelper to update both gene signatures and gene expression profile ID, this may reduce their ability to distinguish TB subtypes across multiple studies.
